items.title: Wike questions Obi’s humility over IDP camp visits
items.description: Sekinat Osundiji Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, has questioned the sincerity of Peter Obi’s visits to internally displaced persons (IDP) camps, suggesting that politicians may use displays of compassion to win public support ahead of the 2027 elections. Wike made the remarks on Thursday at the first Idoma Hall of Fame induction ceremony in Abuja, organised in collaboration with Ochetoha K’Idoma as part of the Idoma Centenary Plus celebration. The minister challenged the perception of Obi as a humble politician, citing the former Anambra governor’s visits to IDP camps, including one he made to mark his 62nd birthday in Plateau State in 2023. “Politicians can tell lies,” Wike said. “A man who did not celebrate his birthday when he was a governor now wants to be president and wants to celebrate his birthday in IDP camps? And you say, ‘Oh, he is very humble’. Which humility is that?” Obi, the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), recently said he had visited 12 IDP camps across the country in recent weeks. During a visit to the Ramin Kura IDP camp in Sokoto State, he shared pictures of himself interacting with children and described it as his 12th visit. The former governor also called on the government to improve conditions in the camps and urged political office holders to spend their holidays in Nigeria to experience the hardships faced by vulnerable citizens. Wike, however, warned Nigerians against being swayed by politicians who adopt public displays of modesty while seeking political office. He cited politicians who suddenly buy roasted corn and groundnuts in public or visit filling stations to comment on fuel prices, describing such gestures as attempts to appeal to voters. “You see a man who has never bought corn on the road suddenly buying corn and groundnuts in public. Who are you deceiving?” he asked. The FCT minister also urged Nigerians to assess the current administration’s performanceagainst the conditions that prevailed before it took office. Acknowledging the country’s economic and security challenges, Wike said the government’s efforts to address them should be considered before voters make political choices. “Nobody is happy that we are where we are. But if we are to trace our steps back to where we are coming from, are there attempts to improve the situation?” he said. He urged Nigerians to ignore politicians he described as “gamblers” as the country approaches the 2027 general election. The post Wike questions Obi’s humility over IDP camp visits appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Karachi court acquits alleged drug baroness Anmol alias Pinky in two more drug cases
items.description: KARACHI: A district and sessions court in Karachi on Friday acquitted alleged drug queenpin Anmol alias Pinky in two narcotics cases. The first case was registered with the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) in 2018 while the second case was registered at the Gizri police station in 2021. Anmol, who had been declared a proclaimed offender in both drug cases, had filed separate applications Section 265-K (power of Court to acquit accused at any stage) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for her acquittal. She appeared before the South additional and sessions judge via a video link at the hearing of her applications today, and the court acquitted her citing a lack of evidence in both cases. The court ordered her release from jail if she was not required in any other case. Her brother, Nasir, has already been acquitted in the 2018 case. In August, a sessions court had acquitted Anmol in three narcotics cases registered at Karachi’s Gizri police station. Anmol’s arrest came to light in May when she appeared before a Karachi court. The arrest was made in connection with two cases, pertaining to the possession of drugs and an unlicensed weapon, registered at Karachi’s Garden police station. The incident gained attention when a video of her being escorted to court without handcuffs went viral on social media.

items.title: Ghana Association of University Administrators suspends nationwide strike
items.description: The Ghana Association of University Administrators (GAUA) has suspended its nationwide strike, effective Friday, October 16, 2026. Members are therefore to report to work from Monday, October 19. The association says the decision was taken after final engagement with the Ministry of Education, with a firm assurance to address all their concerns. The association embarked on the industrial action over concerns about disparities in revised market premiums and related allowances between teaching and non-teaching senior staff in public universities. The strike, which was reactivated on August 10, followed persistent concerns over remuneration differences between the two categories of university staff. The suspension of the industrial action is expected to pave the way for a return to normal administrative operations at public universities across the country. Further details on the terms of the suspension and any agreements reached with the relevant authorities are yet to be confirmed.

Gov Diri didn’t speak on Coastal Highway as local champion — Murray-Bruce replies Duke
items.description: By Bayo Wahab Former senator Ben Murray-Bruce has faulted Donald Duke over his description of Bayelsa State Governor Douye Diri as a “local champion” in the debate over the feasibility of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway. Murray-Bruce said Diri was speaking as a statesman who recognised the value of infrastructure built to international standards, insisting that the governor’s support for the project was not based on a narrow state-level perspective. He stated this in a series of posts on X on Friday while reacting to the exchange between Duke, the presidential candidate of the Peoples Redemption Party, PRP, and Diri over the coastal highway project. Duke had questioned the feasibility and affordability of constructing the highway through Bayelsa’s swampy terrain, prompting the governor to defend the project and highlight his administration’s experience in building roads and bridges across swamps and mangroves. Responding to Duke’s criticism, Diri, through his Chief Press Secretary, Daniel Alabrah, said the former Cross River State governor was not abreast of developments in road construction and infrastructure in Bayelsa. “Clearly, he is not abreast of current developments in road construction and infrastructure development in our state,” Diri said. However, Duke, speaking during an interview on Arise Television on Thursday, dismissed the governor’s defence, arguing that Diri was considering the project from a state-level perspective rather than its broader implications for Nigeria. “The governor of Bayelsa, if he did say so, I don’t know the fellow, but if he did say so, I think he’s just being a local champion,” Duke said. Reacting, Murray-Bruce said he was surprised by Duke’s recent comments, recalling that they had travelled together along the coastline where the highway is being constructed and that Duke had previously praised the vision behind the project. “My dear brother Donald Duke, some years ago, you and I travelled along the stretch of the coastline where this road now runs, and I clearly remember your praise for the vision behind it. That is why your recent comments surprised me,” he said. While acknowledging the high cost of the project, Murray-Bruce argued that major infrastructure investments required substantial funding and should be assessed in terms of their long-term benefits. “Yes, the Coastal Highway is expensive. We agree on that. But nothing of lasting value in this world is cheap or free. Great nations are built by leaders willing to make bold, costly investments that will serve generations yet unborn,” he said. He added that President Bola Tinubu had committed to funding the project and was fulfilling that commitment. Murray-Bruce also rejected suggestions that the project was facing funding challenges, saying construction was progressing and describing the quality of the work as “second to none”. “There is no funding shortfall. The work is progressing, and the quality of construction is second to none,” he said. Defending Diri against Duke’s remarks, Murray-Bruce said the Bayelsa governor’s support for the highway reflected an appreciation of its significance beyond his state. “When Governor Douye Diri commended the road, he was not speaking as a local champion; he was speaking as a statesman who recognises infrastructure of international standard when he sees it. I agree with him completely,” he said. Murray-Bruce acknowledged Duke’s right to criticise the project as a presidential candidate but warned against allowing political interests to undermine infrastructure he described as nationally important. “Donald, I understand that you are running for president, and that your statement is political. That is the nature of the season, and I respect your right to make your case to Nigerians. But we must be careful never to undermine a project of national importance, or the President delivering it, simply for political advantage,” he said. Comparing the highway to the United States’ space programme, he argued that costly projects could still be necessary for national development. “When mankind went to the moon, it was neither cheap nor free. But it was necessary. So is this road,” Murray-Bruce said. The post Gov Diri didn’t speak on Coastal Highway as local champion — Murray-Bruce replies Duke appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Procès d’Algassimou Diallo : les Chambres réunies de la Cour suprême constatent l’absence de ses avocats, accèdent à sa demande et renvoient l’audience sine die
items.description: Le procès d’Algassimou Diallo, ancien avocat général près la Cour suprême, poursuivi notamment pour « provocation à la discrimination, à la haine ou à la violence », s’est poursuivi ce vendredi 16 octobre 2026 devant les Chambres réunies de la haute juridiction. Appelé à la barre pour s’expliquer sur les charges retenues contre lui, l’accusé, vêtu d’une tenue traditionnelle de type « Macky Sall » et la tête rasée, a rappelé à la Cour que ses conseils avaient suspendu leur participation. Il a souligné qu’en matière pénale, il lui était impossible de présenter sa défense dans de telles conditions. L’ancien magistrat a précisé n’avoir disposé d’aucun temps d’échange avec ses conseillers juridiques depuis la suspension de l’audience la veille. Il a ainsi sollicité un report auprès des Chambres réunies afin de pouvoir se concerter avec sa défense. Le ministère public, représenté par Sidy Souleymane N’Diaye et Sidiki Kanté, ne s’est pas opposé à cette demande. Lors de son intervention, le procureur Sidy Souleymane N’Diaye a rappelé que la Constitution et le Code de procédure pénale disposent clairement qu’en matière criminelle, l’assistance d’un ou de plusieurs avocats est obligatoire pour garantir les droits de la défense. « Ce que l’accusé vient de faire valoir est prescrit et protégé par la loi fondamentale », a-t-il affirmé. Pour finir, Sidy Souleymane N’Diaye s’est engagé à faciliter les démarches nécessaires pour qu’Algassimou Diallo puisse s’entretenir avec ses conseils. Afin de garantir la régularité de la procédure, les Chambres réunies de la Cour suprême, présidées par Ibrahima Sory I Tounkara, ont pris acte de l’absence des avocats de la défense et ont prononcé le renvoi de l’audience sine die. Mamadou Yaya Barry L’article Procès d’Algassimou Diallo : les Chambres réunies de la Cour suprême constatent l’absence de ses avocats, accèdent à sa demande et renvoient l’audience sine die est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Musing Ourselves to Death
items.description: C lose your eyes, and imagine a frictionless day. You wake up to a notification that a grocery-store employee will deliver all of the ingredients for the three recipes you saved last night to your “Weeknight Dinner” folder. While you brew your coffee, a program browses online retailers to compare toilet-paper prices, and another solicits competitive bids for Sheetrock work you need done in the garage. During your commute, a bot moves your upcoming dentist appointment to avoid a scheduling conflict. On your lunch break, you get an alert that computers acting on your behalf noticed some unclaimed funds and class-action payouts in a state database and claimed them. Also, the machine has negotiated a cheaper internet plan. By the time you get home, the groceries are on your doorstep, and you’ve gotten back $150. This is the future that OpenAI, Meta, xAI, Google, and the rest are selling with a spate of always-on AI assistants that work for you. “Imagine every person on earth with a second mind beyond their own,” Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, wrote of the company’s new AI helper, Muse. A few weeks after Muse’s launch, OpenAI launched its competing product, Dots, which Sam Altman claimed would let you “get more of your time and attention back.” [ Read: The singularity is not what it seems ] These AI agents promise to bulldoze the inefficiencies of daily life. Think about all of the opportunities you’re currently leaving on the table: You don’t change cell-service providers for a flash sale because of the paperwork involved. You haven’t fiddled with your 401(k) investments in years. You have kids to pick up, a date to dress for, sleep to catch up on. But your AI agents are different—they’re relentless, tireless, and shameless. They work in the background, without supervision, eagerly helping with all of these tasks and a bunch you didn’t even ask for. They use every tactic and loophole at their disposal to get you the best price and the highest-quality service because they’re able to pay attention to everything at once. The AI companies see a massive opportunity for hyper-personalized agents to become a new intermediary layer for the internet and the physical world. This future is already unfolding: People are giving Muse access to their phone number, email, credit cards, and bank accounts to make dinner reservations, contact customer service, and book vacations. Mark Zuckerberg says that he is using Muse to coach his martial-arts form and help him bake with his daughter (he isn’t very familiar with baking, being “normally into smoking meats”). Silicon Valley’s vision of boundless efficiency is shortsighted, or at least incomplete. Near the end of his blog post about Muse, Wang writes that “we’ve never seen humanity with every single person’s agency fully switched on.” He paints a utopian vision of laptop-class optimization. But such frictionless commerce, if it ever does come to pass, could bring about something else entirely: chaos. T he era of the agentic web started less than 24 months ago. Anthropic’s Claude Code, introduced in early 2025, allowed agents to write software and use other programs on your laptop. OpenClaw, launched later that same year, could navigate the web on your behalf. In the spring of 2026, Instinct, an invite-only app that let users text requests to a bot over iMessage or WhatsApp, began capturing the imagination of Silicon Valley insiders. It could book museum tickets, purchase gifts, and find in-network doctors. But it wasn’t until the launch of Meta’s Muse in early September that personalized agents hit the mainstream. Muse has been downloaded more than 5 million times in the past month and is especially popular among early adopters—entrepreneurs, investors, software developers. These users are now reporting back on their experiences and offering previews of our potential agentic future, which sounds both strange and jagged. When we reached out to Rajan Lukose, a start-up founder in the Bay Area, to discuss his use of AI assistants, he had his Muse set up a calendar invite. In the late 1990s and 2000s, Lukose worked for corporate research-and-development teams in Silicon Valley and did early research on web agents. Now, he told us, “they’re actually, finally becoming sort of real.” Lukose has been using Meta’s program for “annoying things that I would never do”: tracking travel sites over time to book the cheapest flights, submitting receipts for DoorDash credits, sorting out problems with a magazine subscription. “That’s something that’s a real pain in the ass that just gets done,” he said. Lukose said that the primary upside of using an agent is clawing back time and money. A few years ago, for instance, Lukose installed an automated tool that went through his Gmail, looked at various transactions, and filed claims under price-purchase guarantees. “That was like $600 that I just would not have gotten myself,” he said. The agentic era promises to deliver those kinds of savings to everyone. Decades ago, the internet was supposed to create perfect markets, with users able to compare the cost and quality of products and services from anywhere in the world. But it failed: People continued to make lots of decisions based on habit. That, in turn, is good for business. “A lot of things online are premised on limited human attention,” Andrey Fradkin, an economist at Boston University, told us. Digital advertisements, recommendation algorithms, brand reputation, and celebrity endorsements steered consumers toward making suboptimal purchases. AI agents are now here to finally fulfill the promise of perfect commerce. “The agent knows your preferences; they can go to every single platform, find the best products, the best deal for you, and then help you make that purchase,” Fradkin said. The agent won’t be fooled by sponsored posts or give up on shopping when they get distracted or hungry. “The current attention-based economy—if you gain the eyeball, you have a better chance to sell certain goods—that may change,” Ken Huang, who studies agentic AI at the University of San Francisco and runs an AI consultancy, told us. The bots are impervious to human-targeted nudges. Their attention is infinite. In the short term, however, this automated quest for efficiency is creating some unsettling dynamics. Over the past month, X, Reddit, and other forums have been overrun with examples of agents haggling customer-service representatives and contractors. Take the case of the Muse user Luke Whiting, who sent his agent to check on a prescription at Walgreens. Whiting, who works for an open-source-database company in San Francisco, told us that the pharmacist at the other end of the call refused to speak to an AI system. His Muse suggested that the best way forward would be for Whiting to abandon using the agent altogether: “Honest take: other stores might say the same thing,” it said. Having the Muse call other pharmacies “could just burn time. The fastest path is probably you calling yourself.” On a Subreddit for call-center employees, a recent thread is titled, in all caps, “I AM NOT AI.” “I have been asked 3 times this week ‘are you human?’” one person replied. Other users who identify themselves as call-center workers discuss their frustrations. One says that when customers question whether they’re talking to AI, they like to respond, “I’m a real boy,” like Pinocchio. Another, fed up with rude callers, vented, “Customers deserve ai.” Companies, meanwhile, are starting to tap AI systems to squeeze more out of their customers. According to Fradkin, many hospitals don’t charge as much as they could, simply because medical-billing codes are countless and labyrinthine. But using AI to document and code patient visits reliably allows hospitals to charge for more, and more expensive, services. That likely contributed to patient costs increasing by $650 million across Blue Cross Blue Shield from 2023 to 2025. And that’s only the beginning; health payments are projected to rise another 9 percent next year, largely because of AI billing. McDonald’s is reportedly using AI to analyze millions of consumer transactions and adjust prices at each location, for each menu item, based on local demand. (McDonald’s has said that its pricing portal is “a tool, not a mandate” to help franchisees.) It’s not hard to imagine vendors using AI to develop personalized, on-demand inventory management and dynamic pricing to maximize profits for streaming subscriptions, sports tickets, drug prescriptions, consumer electronics, insurance policies, and loans. This optimization assumes that the agents work as intended. So far, there have been plenty of stumbles: In a paper published earlier this year, a group of AI researchers found that agents, given assistant-style tasks in a virtual environment, leaked Social Security numbers and were easily hijacked by other people. Agents powered by Chinese models refused to complete tasks that involved politically sensitive topics. Two weeks ago, a tech executive’s AI agent randomly posted his financial information in a workplace chatroom for employees to see. Things could get weirder still: Tech companies market their agents as perfectly rational, when, in actuality, they can be extremely erratic and unpredictable. Sophia Kazinnik, who studies AI agents at Stanford, found some models to be overly generous and others to be exceedingly greedy. Across the board, they were far less patient than humans. When two personal AI agents are haggling over prices in the wild, the outcomes might not be maximally profitable. And there’s no assurance that all future agents will be created equal: More powerful models may have an upper hand in negotiations. Even if the agents are able to effectively shop and negotiate for us, important rules governing the privacy rights, liability, and economic allegiance associated with these tools will have to be codified. Does your Muse have a fiduciary responsibility to you, or a legal responsibility to Meta? If Muse pays for a $2,000 espresso machine instead of a $200 one, can you be refunded? If Muse leaks your account and routing numbers, is Chase required to refund any fraudulent payments? A t some point, everyone’s agents could reach parity. “Just like today, every business has a website and social-media accounts and email addresses and all these things, every business is going to have agents too,” Zuckerberg said in an interview this week. In this future, communication and commerce function almost entirely via computer proxies. Your agent calls a fancy restaurant for a dinner reservation, and a digital maître d’ picks up. Your agent and your insurer’s agent and your hospital’s agent all negotiate the price for your recent appointment. Prices fall, buyers and sellers are better matched, and businesses are incentivized to deliver higher-quality, customized services and products. This is “what economists dream about,” Fradkin said. But friction can serve a purpose for businesses. Banks make great sums when customers leave money in low-interest checking or savings accounts, and studies show that sizable portions of retailer subscription revenue are driven purely by “inertia,” another way of saying that people forget to cancel. (Friction can help consumers too: Inattention and incomplete information at times lead landlords, pharmacies, and other businesses to undercharge.) Our entire economy and basically every company are structured around the notion that humans have mental and physical limitations. Without them, existing market structures could collapse. “There’s this strange protection provided by the inefficiencies in our economy,” Rory Van Loo, a lawyer and a professor at the Wharton School, told us recently. In 2019, well before the rise of large language models, Van Loo envisioned a phenomenon he dubbed “digital market perfection.” Imagine everyone has a digital agent that is always looking for a lower price or a newer, better service. In this world, Van Loo argues, agents could, all at once, direct millions of consumers toward a new product or service—a process he calls “hyperswitching.” That would in theory be good news for consumers, but it would be sheer hell for companies. The nightmare scenario that Van Loo and others have conjured is a style of agentic bank run, where similarly attentive agents all pull money from a bank at once to get their clients better interest rates elsewhere. Maybe this sounds good or exciting to you—a kind of consumer’s revenge—but in practice, stable commercial markets would begin to look and function like the stock market. “If, all of a sudden, people could purchase whatever they wanted at the lowest price with the perfect ability to see every possible option, there’d be a lot of volatility in the world. It would seem highly efficient from an economic standpoint, but it could have devastating effects,” Van Loo said. Picture 1 million personal agents all switching their consumers to a new brand of paper towels on Amazon because a markdown made them three cents cheaper. The same Sweetgreen salad is $18 one week and $38 the next. Your electric bill is $150 one month and $450 the month after, and you’re uncertain with each payment whether your local utility is about to go bankrupt. “Stocks are bought and sold fast; markets change and plummet—ssuch that we have a stop button for it, because it can go off the rails,” Van Loo noted. “But we don’t have those kinds of protections in most other markets.” There’s potential for collateral damage everywhere. If millions of people switching to higher-yield accounts causes a bank run, that’s a disaster for any person or institutional investor with money locked up at that bank. If half of Verizon’s customers switch to AT&T in one week to take advantage of a flash sale, the business could collapse overnight, affecting the other half of its customers. Sometimes, this rapid switching could signal healthy competition. Other times, it could cause organizations to implode. A world where AI proxies do the planning and talking could also mean a future where humans are constantly surprised by things they once were able to anticipate: a birthday present for your spouse ordered in a preposterous size that you must try to explain; a plumber showing up out of the blue. Or perhaps none of this will happen. It’s possible that an assistant-dominated economy turns out to be far more mundane, defined by tacked-on fees to keep the agents in check. Instead of agents allowing you to negotiate and bring down health-care, insurance, and electrical bills, the companies responsible for all of these services charge your agents every time they request to pull your data. Banks, to bolster their revenues in the event of a bank run, institute new and higher fees on checking accounts. Amazon, unable to profit from dynamic pricing and ads in the face of perfectly rational agents, raises prices for consumers and takes a bigger cut from manufacturers. “Generally, if one fee goes away, you get another,” Fradkin said. In other words, everything could be faster, easier, and more efficient for the consumer—but potentially more expensive. Van Loo said that the bigger AI companies will eventually find ways to strike deals with platforms via these protocols, negotiating access, commissions, and partnerships in ways that benefit the companies, not necessarily the consumers. This could result in a sort of preferential treatment like the deals already in place between Meta and Walmart, Sephora, and other retailers, which will effectively cause Muse to prioritize their products. Taking another approach, Amazon has blocked Muse and encourages visitors to browse with its own agent, “Alexa for Shopping,” meaning the company is basically negotiating on both sides of the deal. Meanwhile, this week, JPMorgan announced that it would not allow Instinct, Muse, or other agents into customer accounts. Ultimately, this might all lead to “the same old heavily obstructed, inefficient world we have now,” Van Loo said. “But it will look far more efficient, because it will save some people time and feel much more convenient.” Very powerful companies will design new structures for markets and the internet, determining what can be sold, by whom, and for how much—as they always have. For all the time and money the agentic future could save us, the technology entails another sort of cost: an additional layer of abstraction and disengagement. We’ve largely outsourced our decision making to a small number of platforms: Amazon guides our shopping; Google Maps steers us toward certain restaurants and primary-care providers; Instagram dictates our news consumption. We are told that these recommendations and ads are, based on troves of personal data, already optimal. The companies pushing agents assure us that the decision making will now be even more rational and the deals even better. But checking these claims for ourselves will be harder, because the logic behind those recommendations will be buried in large-language-model chains of reasoning. Eventually, the skeptical instinct to check agents’ work could atrophy altogether. Over time, humans will play a smaller and smaller role in their own life. In the age of the algorithm, it’s easy to throw out cliché terms such as late-stage capitalism in an attempt to describe the extractive, inhumane dynamics of the economy. But what is an agentic future if not the furthest extension of our current market logic? A future of capitalism so perfect, so efficient, that it doesn’t need us at all.

items.title: Quatre interpellations et une importante saisie de cannabis dans deux opérations antidrogue
items.description: Trois individus ont été interpellés à Korhogo, en Côte d'Ivoire, pour «détention illicite» et vente de cannabis et de comprimés de Tramadol, tandis qu’un autre a été arrêté à Guiglo avec cinq kilogrammes de cannabis. Ces interventions, menées dans le cadre de l’opération «Épervier Spécial», ont permis aux forces de police ivoiriennes de saisir plusieurs produits stupéfiants. La lutte contre le trafic de drogue se poursuit en Côte d’Ivoire. Le Groupe de répression anti-drogue (GRAD) a mené deux interventions distinctes à Korhogo et à Guiglo, aboutissant à l’interpellation de quatre individus et à la saisie de cannabis ainsi que de comprimés de Tramadol. Selon une note de la Direction générale de la Police nationale de Côte d’Ivoire (DGPN), publiée le jeudi 15 octobre 2026, la première opération s’est déroulée le mercredi 14 octobre à Korhogo, dans le nord du pays. Elle faisait suite à des renseignements signalant l’existence d’un point de vente de cannabis dans un bas-fond situé entre les quartiers Sinistré et Soba. Pour vérifier ces informations et procéder à d’éventuelles interpellations, trois équipages du GRAD ont été déployés sur les lieux. L’intervention a permis d’interpeller en flagrant délit trois individus identifiés par les initiales Y.F.J., âgé de 20 ans, S.G.A. et C.Z.A., tous deux âgés de 19 ans. La fouille des lieux et des suspects a conduit à la découverte de cinq blocs de cannabis, de deux ballons de cannabis de type «OG-KUSH», de 16 pochons de la même variété et de 11 comprimés de Tramadol dosés à 250 mg. Une seconde intervention a été menée par le GRAD dans la localité de V16, à Guiglo, dans le cadre d’une opération de recherche et de destruction de fumoirs. Elle a abouti à l’interpellation d’un homme âgé de 34 ans et à la saisie de cinq kilogrammes de cannabis. Ces deux opérations s’inscrivent dans le cadre de l’opération «Épervier Spécial», mise en œuvre pour lutter contre le trafic et la circulation des stupéfiants. Elles illustrent la poursuite des actions de la Police nationale ivoirienne contre les réseaux de distribution de drogues et les lieux servant à leur consommation. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Quatre interpellations et une importante saisie de cannabis dans deux opérations antidrogue est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Niger : 5 milliards de dollars de recettes pétrolières réclamés aux partenaires chinois
items.description: Le Niger hausse le ton face a ses partenaires petroliers chinois. Les autorites nigeriennes ont donne un delai de 45 jours a trois societes – la China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC), la West African Oil Pipeline Company (WAPCO) et la Societe de raffinage de Zinder (SORAZ) – pour remedier aux manquements constates dans l'execution de leurs engagements envers l'etat. L'ultimatum a ete annonce par le ministre nigerien des Affaires etrangeres Bakary Yaou Sangare, qui preside le comite charge des negociations sur les questions petrolieres. Dans une declaration lue le 14 octobre a la television publique, il a indique que le comite avait notifie aux trois entreprises des demandes precises a satisfaire sous 45 jours. Au cœur du differend figure le rapatriement des recettes issues des exportations de petrole brut. Selon le ministre, plus de 3 000 milliards de francs CFA, soit environ 5,1 milliards de dollars, n'auraient pas ete rapatries au Niger depuis le debut des exportations en avril 2024. Ce montant correspond a des recettes dont les autorites reclament le transfert, et non necessairement a une dette directe de la CNPC envers l'etat. Un manque a gagner pour le Tresor et les banques Bakary Yaou Sangare a evalue a 17,4 milliards de francs CFA le manque a gagner enregistre par le Tresor public en raison de cette situation. Il a egalement affirme que les banques nigeriennes avaient ete privees de quelque 3 000 milliards de francs CFA de depots, ainsi que des capacites de financement correspondantes. Le ministre a par ailleurs precise que le taux de rapatriement des recettes d'exportation du Niger s'etablissait a 6 %, contre une moyenne superieure a 70 % dans les autres pays de l'Union economique et monetaire ouest-africaine (UEMOA). a l'expiration du delai fixe, l'etat entend tirer « toutes les consequences » du respect ou du non-respect des exigences formulees, a averti le responsable. Au moment de la publication des premieres informations, aucune reaction de la CNPC n'avait ete rapportee. Un partenariat strategique sous pression La CNPC est un partenaire majeur du Niger dans l'exploitation petroliere. Presente dans le pays depuis 2008, l'entreprise chinoise a commence a y produire du petrole en 2011. Le brut destine au marche interieur est notamment traite par la SORAZ, tandis que les exportations s'appuient sur un oleoduc reliant les champs petroliers d'Agadem, dans l'est du Niger, au port beninois de Seme-Kpodji. La construction de cette infrastructure de pres de 2 000 kilometres a ete portee par la WAPCO. Ce differend survient quelques mois apres la conclusion, en mai 2026, d'un protocole de partenariat entre Niamey et les entreprises chinoises, a l'issue d'une periode de tensions et de negociations. Le gouvernement nigerien cherche notamment a faire respecter les engagements contractuels et a accroître les retombees economiques locales de l'exploitation des hydrocarbures. items.title: Dr. Mohammed Amin Adam writes: Ghana’s 2026 domestic debt financing
items.description: Ghana’s recent public debt situation appears to have improved, but the central policy question is whether the debt position and financing system have become durable, transparent, and market based. The recovery has benefited from debt-service relief under the DDEP, external restructuring, IMF programme discipline, expenditure compression, favourable gold prices, and domestic policy measures. These supports have eased immediate pressure, but they do not by themselves remove refinancing risks. The decisive test is whether Government can meet obligations, finance budget deficits, and extend maturities without accumulating arrears, suppressing investor returns, relying on opaque placements, or weakening the domestic yield curve. Since the DDEP, debt has also been managed through a widening set of tools outside regular competitive auctions: reopenings and possible placements of DDEP bonds, non-cash issuance, payment-in-kind coupons, Sinking Fund prefunding, and a planned liability-management programme. Read analysis below Ghana’s 2026 Domestic Debt Financing Download

items.title: 2027: Tinubu afraid to face Nigerians, has no business seeking re-election — ADC campaign
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike, Abuja The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has accused President Bola Tinubu of being afraid to face Nigerians, saying his reported decision not to campaign across all 36 states ahead of the 2027 election amounts to contempt for the electorate. The council said the move could give its presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, an advantage, arguing that Nigerians deserve a leader willing to defend his record, answer questions and explain his plans for the country. The ADC-PCC Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, stated this while receiving a delegation of youths under the aegis of Young Voters for Atiku (YVA). Ologbondiyan said a president seeking re-election should be prepared to meet voters and account for his performance, rather than rely on official engagements as a reason to avoid nationwide campaigning. “What President Tinubu has done is a clear act of contempt against the Nigerian people. The APC is known for its contempt for Nigerians. How can a man who wants to be re-elected as president, after failing woefully, say he does not want to visit the people he seeks to govern? It is an aberration of norm,” he said. He rejected the argument that official duties could prevent Tinubu from campaigning nationwide, citing former Nigerian presidents Olusegun Obasanjo, Goodluck Jonathan and Muhammadu Buhari, as well as American presidential candidates Donald Trump and Kamala Harris. “Saying that he (Tinubu) will be attending to official assignments is untrue, fake, deceitful and insincere. Didn’t former Presidents Olusegun Obasanjo, Goodluck Jonathan and Muhammadu Buhari attend to official duties while campaigning for their return tickets? Didn’t Donald Trump campaign? Didn’t Kamala Harris campaign? Why is Tinubu’s case different?” Ologbondiyan queried. He further alleged that public anger over hunger, poverty, insecurity and economic hardship explained the president’s reported reluctance to engage voters across the country. “He knows Nigerians are hungry and angry. He knows that the average Nigerian finds it difficult to eat and to be secure. He has failed on all fronts, so he is afraid to face Nigerians. He is running away from the reality he created,” he said. Ologbondiyan urged young Nigerians to reject the APC in 2027, warning that another term for the ruling party would prolong the hardship citizens were experiencing. “I appeal to every young Nigerian to reject them. Let us collectively reject hunger, reject poverty, reject hardship and reject insecurity. The APC has brought only pain to Nigerians. It is time to say enough is enough,” he said. He described Atiku as physically fit and mentally alert, saying the former vice-president was prepared to campaign across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory. He also pledged that an ADC government would pursue economic recovery, wealth creation, improved security and better living standards. “Atiku Abubakar will bring back subsidy to reduce cost of petroleum products, create wealth, end hunger in our land, secure our nation and restore our battered economy. He has the experience, the capacity and the compassion to rescue Nigeria. He is fit, ready and prepared to lead Nigeria out of this present predicament,” Ologbondiyan added. The ADC-PCC also claimed that the inauguration of the APC Presidential Campaign Council had strengthened its own political standing, alleging that the event attracted no endorsements from ADC members or sympathisers. The post 2027: Tinubu afraid to face Nigerians, has no business seeking re-election — ADC campaign appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Consultations : Le MP affirme n’avoir reçu aucune proposition de participation au gouvernement
items.description: À l’issue des consultations menées avec Fatima Zahra El Mansouri, chargée de former le prochain gouvernement, le Parti du Mouvement populaire (MP) affirme n’avoir reçu aucune proposition de participation et n’en avoir formulé aucune de son côté. La formation dirigée par Ouzzine entend ainsi maintenir son positionnement dans l’opposition, estimant que les échanges engagés n’ont pas dépassé le stade des discussions générales et des marques de courtoisie. Dans un communiqué publié à l’issue de la réunion de son bureau politique, mercredi 14 octobre, sous la présidence de son secrétaire général, Mohamed Ouzzine, et en présence du président du parti, Mohand Laenser, le MP précise que les consultations, organisées en deux rounds, n’ont débouché sur aucune proposition susceptible de justifier un changement de position politique. Le parti affirme avoir participé à ces échanges « dans un esprit positif et avec une ferme volonté de rompre positivement avec la précédente législature gouvernementale ». Il dit avoir défendu une vision globale de la nature du gouvernement attendu par les Marocains, au regard des défis stratégiques, politiques, liés aux droits, économiques, sociaux, territoriaux et identitaires auxquels le pays sera confronté lors de la prochaine étape. Le Mouvement populaire assure n’avoir présenté ni offre ni demande au cours de ces consultations. « Servir le pays » demeure, selon lui, une exigence qui dépasse les positions institutionnelles et les calculs politiques. La formation entend poursuivre son action au sein d’une opposition qu’elle qualifie de constructive, avec l’ambition de proposer une alternative politique et sociétale « sérieuse et efficace », au service des intérêts du pays et de ses citoyens. Le parti a également tenu à démentir les informations relayées par certains sites au sujet de son attitude dans les discussions gouvernementales, dénonçant des allégations et des contrevérités qui, selon lui, ne rendent compte ni de sa réalité ni de l’indépendance de ses choix politiques. Il a, dans le même temps, mis en avant la cohésion de sa direction et de ses bases militantes. Une première évaluation des législatives du 23 septembre La réunion du bureau politique a également été consacrée à un premier examen des résultats des élections législatives organisées le 23 septembre 2026. Le Mouvement populaire a relevé les progrès enregistrés lors de ce scrutin, tout en jugeant que les résultats, malgré leur importance, ne sont pas à la hauteur de la place politique qu’il estime mériter ni du poids qu’il revendique en tant que composante essentielle de l’opposition nationale. Le parti a décidé de poursuivre l’analyse détaillée de son bilan électoral lors de la prochaine session ordinaire de son conseil national. Cette étape devra permettre d’examiner les résultats du scrutin et d’en tirer les enseignements nécessaires sur les plans organisationnel et politique. Kosmos Energy, Eni, TotalEnergies and AGL Win Big at African Energy Awards
items.description: Kosmos Energy Ghana and its CEO, Andrew Inglis, were among the top winners at the 2026 African Energy Awards. Eni, TotalEnergies, and Africa Global Logistics (AGL) were also recognised for their work in entrepreneurship, petroleum production, exploration, renewable energy, and logistics. The awards were presented during African Energy Week in Cape Town, South Africa, celebrating achievements across Africa’s energy sector. Kosmos Energy Ghana received the CSR Project of the Year award for its Kosmos Innovation Centre, and Mr Inglis was given the Mohammed S. Barkindo Lifetime Achievement Award. Eni was named Exploration and Production Leader of the Year, TotalEnergies won Power Africa Developer of the Year, and AGL was recognised as International Service Provider of the Year. Kosmos Energy was recognised for supporting entrepreneurs The CSR award recognised Kosmos Energy Ghana’s support for entrepreneurs through the Kosmos Innovation Centre, which provides mentorship and business development assistance to businesses in Ghana’s agriculture and energy value chains. The initiative aims to help entrepreneurs build commercially viable businesses, strengthen their capacity, and create employment opportunities. Kosmos Energy is a major investor in Ghana’s petroleum industry through its interests in the Jubilee and Tweneboa-Enyenra-Ntomme (TEN) fields. The company is still investing in these fields as Ghana works to reverse declining oil production and attract new investment in its petroleum sector. This recognition shows how private-sector investment can support businesses beyond just oil and gas. For Ghana, it also raises questions about the measurable impact of corporate social investment programmes on business survival, revenue growth and job creation. Kosmos CEO receives lifetime achievement award Mr Inglis was honoured for a career spanning more than four decades in the energy industry. He joined Kosmos Energy in 2014 after spending 30 years at British Petroleum (BP), where he rose to become Chief Executive Officer of its Exploration and Production business. At Kosmos, he has overseen investments in major African energy developments, including the Greater Tortue Ahmeyim liquefied natural gas project involving Mauritania and Senegal, which achieved first LNG production in 2025. His leadership has also been associated with continued investment in Ghana’s Jubilee and TEN fields. The award comes as Ghana seeks to extend the productive life of existing petroleum fields, encourage additional drilling and strengthen domestic natural gas supplies. For the country, sustaining investment will be critical to improving oil production, supporting energy security and maintaining investor confidence. Eni recognised for exploration successes Italian energy company Eni received the Exploration and Production Leader of the Year award for discoveries across its African operations. These discoveries include the Algaita-01 well in Angola’s Block 15/06 and the Murene South-1X well in Block CI-501 offshore Côte d’Ivoire. The Murene South-1X well is part of the larger Baleine development, which started production in 2023. ENI’s operations in Ghana include its flagship integrated oil and natural gas project located off the west coast of Ghana, which utilises the John Agyekum Kufuor floating production, storage, and offloading (FPSO) vessel and an onshore gas plant in Sanzule (Western Region). TotalEnergies wins renewable energy award. TotalEnergies won Power Africa Developer of the Year for its Hydra hybrid energy project in South Africa. The project combines a 216-megawatt solar plant with a battery energy storage system that can store 500 megawatt-hours of electricity. According to the awards announcement, the facility should generate more than 400 gigawatt-hours each year, enough to power over 200,000 homes. AGL recognised for logistics services Africa Global Logistics was named International Service Provider of the Year for its integrated logistics network covering ports, rail, road transport and warehousing. The company supports energy projects from construction to production, moving equipment, materials, and energy products between sites and international markets. Formerly known as Bolloré Africa Logistics, AGL joined the MSC Group in 2022. This recognition shows how important efficient logistics are for cutting costs and supporting energy infrastructure development. The awards highlight the importance of investment in petroleum production, entrepreneurship, exploration, renewable energy and logistics.

items.title: Aircraft loses door shortly after take-off from Abuja
items.description: By Dickson Omobola A CL60 aircraft operated by Triton Aviation has made an emergency landing at the Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport, Abuja, after its crew reported that a door had opened in flight. The aircraft, with registration number T7-SEI, departed Abuja for the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos, at 4:17 on Thursday. The aircraft, according to the serious incident report, was about three nautical miles from the airport and at 3,000 feet when the crew made a “MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY” distress call at 4:20. The crew reported that a door had opened in flight, prompting air traffic control to direct the aircraft back to Abuja for an emergency landing on Runway 22. The report stated: “At 1620 UTC, APP-RADAR informed Tower DWCO52 a CL60 with registration marking T7SEI that departed Abuja at 1617 UTC runway 22 to DNMM at 3 nautical miles outbound, passing 3000ft made a MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY call. DWC052 reported an open door in flight. Radar vectored the aircraft back to land using runway 22. “16:22 UTC, Fire watch room and Medical team informed to be on standby. Information pertaining to the flight passed to the fire watch room. Fire watch asked to position at A4 and A5. “At 16:29 UTC, Abuja Tower was in contact with DWC052, and the crew asked Tower if they could see their door opened. “The Duty air traffic controller (DATCO) used the birocular to view the aircraft but was unable to view the door because of the position of the aircraft, and the crew was advised. At 16:34 UTC, DWC052 landed safely on runway 22. On landing, the fuselage of the aircraft was clearly visible to the DATCO and the door was missing from the aircraft. DWC052 was taxied to the International apron extension. At 1640 UTC, DWC052 reported Marshalar insight and was parked by the marshaller.” The media team of the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau, NSIB, confirmed the serious incident. The team said: “ Yes, it happened. The investigators are there. We will be releasing an official statement shortly.” The post Aircraft loses door shortly after take-off from Abuja appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Dialogue social : le Premier ministre Ahmadou Alhaminou LO demande un moratoire de trois mois sur les grèves
items.description: Le Premier ministre, Ahmadou Alhaminou Mohamed LO, a appelé les partenaires sociaux à privilégier la concertation et annoncé la mise en place, dès décembre 2026, de comités de dialogue social dans tous les ministères. Cette démarche intervient alors que le suivi du Pacte national de stabilité sociale fait état d’un taux de réalisation de 71 % des engagements des parties. Le Premier ministre, Ahmadou Alhaminou Mohamed LO, a demandé aux organisations syndicales d’observer un moratoire de trois mois sur les grèves annoncées, tout en réaffirmant la volonté de l’État de respecter ses engagements. Il s’exprimait jeudi 15 octobre 2026, au Building administratif Président Mamadou DIA, lors d’une réunion du Comité de pilotage tripartite du Pacte national de stabilité sociale pour une croissance inclusive et durable. La rencontre a réuni des membres du Gouvernement, des représentants du patronat et des organisations syndicales autour de l’état d’avancement des engagements pris dans le cadre de ce pacte. Selon le dispositif de suivi-évaluation présenté à cette occasion, le taux de réalisation des engagements du Gouvernement et des partenaires sociaux s’établit à 71 %. Face aux tensions sociales, le chef du Gouvernement a invité les différentes parties à privilégier le dialogue afin de parvenir à des solutions concertées. Il a assuré que les engagements de l’État seraient scrupuleusement respectés, en tenant compte du rétablissement des moyens nécessaires à leur mise en œuvre. Le Premier ministre a également demandé aux syndicats de privilégier la concertation plutôt que le recours à une grève générale, en proposant un moratoire de trois mois pour donner davantage de temps aux discussions et à la recherche de solutions. Pour renforcer ce dispositif, Ahmadou Alhaminou Mohamed LO a annoncé la mise en place, dès décembre 2026, de comités de dialogue social dans l’ensemble des ministères. Cette mesure vise à consolider les mécanismes de concertation entre l’administration et les partenaires sociaux et à favoriser le règlement des différends en amont. Ces annonces s’inscrivent dans la mise en œuvre du Pacte national de stabilité sociale pour une croissance inclusive et durable, qui repose sur l’engagement des pouvoirs publics, des organisations syndicales et du patronat à promouvoir un climat social apaisé. Le taux de réalisation de 71 % constitue un indicateur de l’état d’avancement des engagements pris. La poursuite du dialogue et la concrétisation des mesures restantes demeurent des enjeux importants pour consolider la confiance entre les différentes parties et prévenir de nouvelles tensions sociales.

items.title: The Unpredictable Virus at the Core of Gene Therapy
items.description: In recent months, news came out about several distressing cases that have underscored the risks of gene therapy, which delivers DNA to a patient’s cells to treat disease. All of these cases have one thing in common that’s not apparent at first glance. A child in China , enrolled in a clinical trial for gene therapy, died of acute respiratory distress syndrome, in which fluid builds up in the lungs and oxygen cannot enter. In a separate clinical trial in China, a child died after clots formed in their small blood vessels, likely disrupting the delivery of oxygen to organs such as the kidneys and brain. And earlier this year, researchers reported that a 5-year-old boy treated in Philadelphia had a brain tumor that was likely caused by gene therapy. (He’s doing okay now.) In each of these cases, the gene therapies relied on a versatile but unpredictable type of virus: adeno-associated virus, or AAV for short. AAVs are the workhorses of many of the most successful gene therapies in the world. Scientists modify them so that they can deliver a working copy of particular genes to the body, but cannot replicate and aren’t infectious. These treatments have transformed a form of spinal muscular atrophy—once the genetic disorder most responsible for infant mortality—into a survivable condition, and have been approved for a devastating enzyme deficiency, muscle-wasting disease, and hemophilia, to name a few. The terrible outcomes AAVs can cause are rare, but they’re a real risk. So far, the treatments have been used in small patient groups—the most commonly given one has been received by about 5,000 children since 2019—and focused on diseases that dramatically affect or shorten people’s lives. But AAV-based gene therapies are being explored for prevalent ailments, including heart disease, high blood pressure, and perhaps even Alzheimer’s. As the use of gene therapy increases, so might the instances in which it goes dramatically wrong. The modified AAVs involved in gene therapy each contain a single strand of DNA. One portion of that strand drives the virus’s ability to get inside cells, and another is the helpful human gene that’s being delivered. The viral components are more likely than the therapeutic gene to be unpredictable and can cause side effects. On occasion, for instance, instead of hanging around within cells, AAVs insert themselves into the patient’s genetic code. This seems to have been what happened to the 5-year-old who developed a brain tumor—the AAV put itself into a part of his DNA that then produced the cancer. Hurler syndrome, the condition the boy was being treated for when he received the gene therapy at 13 months old, is progressively debilitating. The syndrome can cause problems for the skeleton, heart, lungs, and liver, and affect cognitive development; life expectancy is short. Many gene therapies are geared toward children for whom a working copy of a vital gene would promise something closer to a healthy life. “We should remember what diseases we are talking about,” Albert Rizvanov, a scientist at Kazan Federal University in Russia who studies gene therapy, told me. For such patients, gene therapy may seem like an obvious choice. But parents are still left weighing the potential benefits of treatment against the real risks, including fatal complications. Jo Kaur and her husband, Richie DiGeorge, faced this question not too long ago. Their son Riaan was born in 2019 weighing less than six pounds, and by the time he was three months of age, they were concerned about his eyesight. Riaan’s pediatrician suspected it was just near-sightedness, Kaur, who has written extensively online about her family’s story, told me, but her “mom radar went off.” She secured an appointment with an ophthalmologist who found that her son had cataracts in both his eyes. Riaan’s overall growth also wasn’t on track, and he was missing milestones. At 15 months old, he was diagnosed with a severe form of Cockayne syndrome, a genetic condition that causes progressive muscle weakness and nerve damage. This diagnosis meant not just that Riaan had problems with his eyes or was growing a little slowly, but that his life would likely be short—perhaps just five to seven years. He could roll and pull his family in for cuddles, but by the time he was 6 years old, at the end of 2025, he was still unable to sit independently for more than a few minutes at a time, or stand or walk independently, or feed himself. He was so small that he was still wearing clothes for 18-month-olds. By then, Riaan had lost a lot of nervous tissue. His brain size was about 50 percent of what would be typical for a child his age. But Kaur and DiGeorge had worked closely with scientists for years to develop a gene therapy for Cockayne syndrome. The hope was to stop or at least slow Riaan’s loss of nerve cells. “Because Cockayne syndrome is neurodegenerative, even an extended period in which Riaan simply remains where he is now would be enormously meaningful to us,” Kaur said. The researchers developing a Cockayne-syndrome treatment for Riaan had done mouse experiments to determine whether the medication was safe and whether it worked. Some of the animals had signs of liver damage, but they also lived longer. Kaur and her husband had been involved in countless meetings and stayed up-to-date on all of the developments. Knowing the risks so intimately increased the weight of the decision to allow Riaan to receive the treatment. “We’d read all the papers, we knew the science,” she said, “but you’re still making a huge decision for your child.” She and her husband were primarily concerned about the treatment’s safety. Ultimately, this past April, they decided to go ahead with the therapy. Riaan would be the first child in the world to receive this treatment for Cockayne syndrome. Surgeons created a small hole in his skull, inserted a catheter, and within minutes delivered the gene therapy to him. When night came, as Kaur wrote in her own account of Riaan’s procedure, she fought the urge to sneeze as he slept on her arm in the hospital. Everything seemed very delicate, and she dared not move. His head had to stay elevated and he “had so many wires,” she told me. “I didn’t want to wake him.” The first successful gene therapy, tested back in 1990, used a nonreplicating version of a mouse virus. But that virus doesn’t readily get into all cells, so scientists kept looking for others to try. One was adenovirus—an attractive option in part because it could deliver working genes to a high number of cells. But in 1999, an 18-year-old named Jesse Gelsinger died shortly after having a severe immunological response to a therapy that used adenovirus to treat his rare metabolic disorder. Gelsinger is believed to have experienced the same acute respiratory distress syndrome that killed one of the patients in China. In that recent trial, the Chinese company HuidaGene Therapeutics was using gene therapy to treat Duchenne muscular dystrophy. In many cases, the body weakness caused by Duchenne leads to death during a child’s teenage years, and families whose kids might benefit from gene therapy have been pushing for it. In the United States, a different AAV-based gene-therapy treatment for Duchenne, made by the company Sarepta, has been controversial in part because of concerns that it may not actually do enough for patients. But it has also been associated with deaths: Last summer, the FDA reported that it was investigating after several patients receiving Sarepta’s therapy succumbed to acute liver failure, a known risk. (After the deaths, in a public statement, HuidaGene extended condolences to the family and reiterated its focus on patient safety. Sarepta paused shipments of treatment for certain patients.) AAVs delivered into the bloodstream are very good at reaching the liver, where they’re filtered out and can accumulate. As a result, the engineered viruses can have a harder time reaching other organ systems and tissues, including muscle. To get to those harder-to-reach parts of the body, sometimes scientists increase the amount of treatment they give. The doses of viral particles in gene therapy can vary so widely that one type of treatment might have a dose of 500 billion functional viral particles per kilogram, and another 300 trillion. (The doses in commonly used drugs tend to occupy a much narrower range.) Many patients have few other options than to risk a bigger dose, Luk Vandenberghe, who was involved in the discovery of a commonly used AAV and now directs the gene-therapy center at the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary, told me. “The alternatives can mean restarting development with a new and modified gene therapy,” he said. Researchers have been trying to test different variants of AAV and engineering the viruses’ shells to get them to reach desired tissues in the body. But that, too, can change how the body reacts. A year ago, a child died in a clinical trial that used an AAV designed with a shell to help it reach the brain and deliver treatment for a congenital seizure disorder. The company behind the trial, Capsida, paused the clinical trial and a few months later said that the child had experienced brain swelling following the infusion. In May, it announced that it had closed the trial. (The company has “been conducting extensive nonclinical work to understand what led to the outcome” and will incorporate its findings into future work, Katherine Carlyle Smith, a Capsida spokesperson, wrote in an email.) Despite the risks of gene therapy, the growing number of people who have received it also means that many people have benefited, without concerning side effects. “Caution is of course always top of mind, but I think the promise of gene therapy overwhelms the risks of not taking action for a lot of parents,” Kaur, Riaan’s mother, told me. She and her husband felt especially cautious about giving Riaan gene therapy, precisely because he had a life-limiting disease: “We want to maintain and preserve the life and happiness that he currently has,” she said. Currently, Riaan is being tapered off his immunosuppressants and monitored closely. In the meantime, Kaur is observing signs that the therapy might be helping. He can sit by himself on the edge of the couch. He still needs support to stand or walk, but he wants to try more often. Kaur knows these observations are anecdotal, but Riaan’s physical therapist has also noticed the changes, she said. He has become more expressive, too—an outcome that surprised Kaur. “He would rarely say ‘mama,’ and now he says it all day long … ‘ma-ma-ma,’” she says. “It’s beautiful to hear.”

items.title: The Cutest Target of Trump’s D.C. Makeover
items.description: When Donald Trump flies over Washington’s East Potomac Park, as he does on his helicopter rides to Joint Base Andrews, he sees a piece of prime waterfront real estate with serious PGA potential . In what might as well be another episode of Extreme Makeover: Capital Edition , the president wants to convert the more than 300-acre man-made island and its affordable golf course into a championship-worthy destination. But it turns out that there’s a lot you can’t perceive from the sky. The park, which Trump visited for 90 minutes in June, buzzes with life. Municipal golfers—hardly the country-club set—trek across the green. Cyclists and runners collect miles on Ohio Drive, the road that circles the wing-shaped island. Fishers and picnickers sit along Hains Point, the park’s tip. Many locals fear that they could lose all of this if the president gets his golf-course glow-up. Although it sits just south of Washington’s expanse of monuments, East Potomac Park isn’t typically a site of controversy. Usually, its biggest moment comes each spring, when its cherry trees blossom. But the attention was less cheerful on Saturday, when the National Park Service went on a sudden tree-chopping spree. The agency cut down more than 400 trees along the course, prompting worries that it might be using maintenance as a cover for beginning work on Trump’s grander plans, which still face bureaucratic hurdles. On Monday, timber was piled up on the golf course. Among the standing trees, I counted about 75 marked with caution tape to save them from the axe. A lone protester held a sign that read Stop Tree Genocide . Ana C. Reyes, the federal judge presiding over a lawsuit about the renovation, lambasted the administration in an emergency court hearing that day, saying that officials had lost all credibility in the case. She has since extended an order to stop the government from clearing trees through October 26 and is requiring the administration to provide three business days’ notice before it makes irreparable changes to the golf course. A lawyer for the government told Reyes that officials had done their best to notify her of their plans ahead of time, as she’d requested. “No, you did not do your best,” Reyes said. “You did your absolute worst.” Few know what will happen to East Potomac Park if Trump gets his way. Full plans for the golf-course project have not been released, and the National Park Service canceled a historic-preservation meeting, which might have offered the public some insight. (The park is on the National Register of Historic Places and is subject to extensive review.) But Trump has given indications that this public park might soon take on a more exclusive air. For many, last year’s sudden East Wing demolition destroyed a symbol of the American people. The plans for East Potomac Park represent something far more tangible; people feel that the White House is trying to seize part of their neighborhood. There’s another, even lesser-known corner of East Potomac Park. Hidden beneath a canopy of trees lies the cutest potential casualty of the renovation projects that have occupied much of Trump’s time during his second term: the country’s oldest continually running mini-golf course. (There are competing claims to that superlative.) It’s a microcosm of a microcosm—the most welcoming place in a park made, by congressional act, for the public. Eric Lee for The Atlantic / Eric Lee Perhaps the reelection of a golf-loving, resort-owning president was always going to affect the three low-cost municipal golf courses in Washington, D.C., which are on land controlled by the National Park Service. Last December, the Trump administration suddenly terminated a nonprofit’s leases to operate the sites. That group, National Links Trust, made a deal with the White House in May to continue running two of the courses long-term and East Potomac Golf Links in the interim, before its White House–led renovation. The president tapped the well-known golf architect Tom Fazio, a longtime collaborator who has worked on a handful of Trump courses, to run the project. Trump criticized the site as “dilapidated, worn out, and very dangerous and outdated” and vowed to turn it into a host site for major tournaments. Creating such a course would likely require taking over almost the whole park. The Washington Post reported last month that Trump has been fixated on eliminating Ohio Drive and extending the course to the island’s edge, a change that could make jogging or cycling around the park impossible. In response to questions about the project, a White House spokesperson told me that Trump would restore its “glamour and prestige,” writing, “As a private citizen, President Trump built some of the greatest golf courses in the world, and he is now extending his unmatched design skills and excellent eye for detail to D.C.’s East Potomac Golf Links.” The Department of the Interior told me that “DOI and NPS are committed to continuing the relationships we have built with the local golf communities to ensure these courses are safe, beautiful, open, affordable, enjoyable, accessible, and world-class for people living in and visiting the greatest capital city in the world.” DOI did not respond when asked a second time about whether the mini-golf course will remain. The attraction did not seem to be included in renderings of the course disseminated by the National Garden of American Heroes Foundation, a Trump-associated fundraising entity. Nor was mini-golf visible on a design of the new course that Trump was photographed holding during his summer tour. Eric Lee for The Atlantic / Eric Lee This may seem like a small problem—mini, even. But the humble course speaks to the broader dismissiveness toward D.C. residents that has characterized Trump’s impositions on the capital. The changes can be felt across the city: the year-plus deployment of National Guard troops on neighborhood streets; the fencing-off of public spaces such as Lafayette Square; the takeover of the Kennedy Center, which has been all but shut down. Municipal golf courses, which are owned or operated by local governments, are known for widening access to a sport associated with the wealthy. Nowhere is this democratic spirit more alive than on a municipal mini-golf course frequented by children, parents, and newbies to the green. Somehow, on my first round of the fun-size sport in more than a decade, I hit a hole in one. I played the mini-golf course this spring with Ryan Moody, a landscape architect who’d worked on a 2024 renovation of the mini course, and Michael McCartin, a co-founder of National Links Trust. As we strolled past the classical-columned clubhouse, Moody mentioned that he was planning to host his son’s fifth-birthday party there; McCartin said that he was pretty sure he’d had his own tenth birthday at the mini-golf course, decades ago. [ Read: The capital is a mess ] The mini course has a retro feel and a simple design that should not be mistaken for technical simplicity. It might be the toughest mini-golf course in the country, McCartin warned. There’s no rating system, he clarified, but whereas newer mini-golf courses are dominated by easier holes, this one is full of elaborate, multistep excursions. Nearly 100 years old, it is blissfully uninterested in granting players instant gratification. Mini-golf conjures images of theme-park kitsch—faux volcanos, towering plastic dinosaurs. With its clean lines, concrete edges, stone walls, and limited color palette, the East Potomac mini-golf course is closer to bureaucracy-core. It has some decorative touches: a loop-de-loop here and a wishing well there, but overall, the atmosphere is understated. You’re supposed to feel like you’re golfing in a garden, Moody told me. As actual golfers took their shots on the larger courses around us, McCartin coached us. At one point, I thought I’d hit another hole in one, but then I discovered that the ball had gone through a hidden tunnel and ended up on another green with even more steps to the actual finish. On another hole, I simply gave up counting my attempts, which were well into the double digits. One hole involved hitting the ball through replicas of nearby landmarks. (You could imagine the addition of a triumphal arch if the course survives.) When I accidentally overshot a ball and it flew over the White House, the U.S. Capitol, and Mount Vernon, my golfing partners let me keep going from where it landed. Jumping over governmental obstacles felt like some kind of metaphor. Eric Lee for The Atlantic / Eric Lee Remote and central at the same time, East Potomac Park provides an escape from city life. Congress designated the site in 1897 “to be forever held and used as a park for the recreation and pleasure of the people.” Alex Rosen, a D.C. resident who recently founded Save East Po, an activist group opposing Trump’s renovation, told me that every addition to the park, such as the cherry trees and Ohio Drive, “has broadened and expanded what it means to have recreation on this peninsula.” The 18-hole mini-golf course opened during the Great Depression and became among the park’s most popular sites. When Moody took on its revamp, the tiny course was in disrepair, but he studied old photos and tried to bring past elements back, such as catenary lighting that once kept the place open late. “It’s respectful of the historic layout of the course,” he said, a layout that has “stood the test of time.” In contrast, the plan for a professional-grade course risks sharing a heavy-handed quality with Trump’s other D.C. projects. Ideas like the triumphal arch are “all sort of plopped down in the landscape, aggressively and without any recognition of continuity of visual and spatial relationships,” Charles Birnbaum, an architect who leads the Cultural Landscape Foundation, a group that has opposed many of Trump’s changes, told me. The mini-golf course may have continuity with the landscape, but if I’m being honest, it does not have continuity with how I like to spend an afternoon. If I could save one feature of East Potomac Park from Trump’s wrecking ball, it would not be the mini. Ohio Drive has my vote. But that’s the beauty of the place. I’m not forcing the golfers to join me on my 10-mile run, and I don’t need to join them with my 10-over-par. In a world where East Potomac Park is doing what Congress intended, no activity needs to be sacrificed for anyone else’s favorite sport.

items.title: Maurice: les habitants de Goodlands entre condamnation des violences et colère contre le gouvernement
items.description: Le retour au calme reste fragile à Maurice après deux nuits de tensions et de violences liées notamment aux problèmes de distribution d’eau et au tir d’un policier sur un véhicule, qui a grièvement blessé en début de semaine une jeune femme de 29 ans rentrant du travail. Le gouvernement a instauré un couvre-feu nocturne, dont la troisième nuit s’achève ce vendredi matin. À Goodlands, dans le nord de l’île, les habitants oscillent entre condamnation des débordements et colère contre le gouvernement.
