items.title: ‘Revolution, the dirty word’: On Lara Baladi’s Z for Zarafa
items.description: What happens after revolution? How do we remember, if we do at all? In her exhibition, Z for Zarafa, which opened at Gypsum Gallery at the start of June and closed on September 23, Lara Baladi takes us through a scavenger hunt of moments, leading us into an archive of revolution, specifically looked at from an aftermath vantage point of movement, migration, displacement and the ultimate wrestling for freedom. The exhibition acts as a physical installation of aspects of an online database, Anatomy of Revolution , which is a project exploring the various iconography and language of resistance movements. The database consolidates research, visual, written and audio material from past and present global struggles, which Baladi gathered between 2011 and 2021 as part of her project, Vox Populi, Tahrir Archives . The body of data, a vast space of references, is organized into an abecedary using the Arabic alphabet, designed to work as “an educational primer of struggles for freedom.” The exhibition, a multi-year effort through a wide network of collaborations, brought together the works of editors, writers and visual artists reflecting on experiences of migration and exile, alongside the works of refugee women in Cairo, blacksmiths in Imbaba, antiquaries in downtown Cairo, embroiderers in Islamic Cairo and potters in Fayoum, among others. The opening day marked the launch of the first edition of The Anatomist, a publication “befriending” themes of “displacement, borders, exile and return” through commissioned articles and testimonies, a “companion” to the exhibition. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. In the website abecedary, if we jump to the letter Z, we find the story of a giraffe named Zarafa, a diplomatic gift sent from Mohamed Ali Pasha to King Charles X in 1826. She was captured by hunters in Sennar, Sudan before being taken to France. Destined for a life of spectacle, she, along with her handler Hassan al-Berbery, made the arduous journey to Paris, crossing the sea through Alexandria and Marseille, to satisfy a cosmetic political urge: first by camel, then aboard a felucca, before embarking a ship and then completing a 900 km journey on foot. Once in Marseille, she had to be hidden out of fear of her premature discovery, so the walk to Paris was completed at night with her head and eyes covered. It took 32 days. She would be the first giraffe in France. Once Zarafa arrived at the destination at the Jardins des Plantes in Paris, she sparked a cultural and fashion frenzy. People would line up to see her, feed her petals, celebrate her, even dress like her. She lived the rest of her life for the next 18 years confined in the beautiful yet estranging garden, available to the public for entertainment. “ Forced out of her home in Sudan and into an estranged existence in France ,” Zarafa, or Zoo-Zoo as her handler would call her, becomes a metaphor for migration. The story and image of Zarafa and how it generated a cultural frenzy are our entry point to the exhibition, capturing the transformation, or recognition, of an image becoming a symbol that garners a collective shared meaning and response. This shift in meaning is examined through the exhibition’s main reflection on migration and return; we start to explore stories of movement and the political and personal dimensions of cultural exchange before the physical experience takes us through historical, present and personal stories of migration and displacement. These confounded layers of movement, exchange, migration and displacement lead us into a portal to Baladi’s data on struggles for freedom, of which Zarafa is an excerpt. At the exhibition’s entrance, we are faced with For Glory of the Wind and Water, a tapestry holding moments woven through fabric, depicting tragedies which have seared through minds and into the public consciousness, like the viral image of Aylan Kurdi, the three-year-old Syrian toddler who was found dead on a Turkish beach in 2015. He, his five-year-old brother and their mother drowned in the Mediterranean minutes into the dangerous journey of trying to escape from Syria to Greece. In the tapestry, we also see images selected by Baladi, like Dorothea Lange’s Migrant Mother , a photo which became a global symbol of the Great Depression, taken in 1936 of a farmworker and her children at a pea picker camp in California. Zarafa appears in the tapestry in illustrations of her travels by boat and her arrival to France. Beside these images, stories of marginalized refugee women are woven into the fabric, following a series of workshops with them, led by Baladi and organized in collaboration with nongovernmental organization Threads of Hope. Scenes of protest are also seen in the tapestry. With all of these elements, the tapestry becomes a collage of documented experiences, taking the audience through multiple stories at once. It introduces a simultaneity in how we engage with themes of struggle, movement and belonging. The tactility in the tapestry reflects Baladi’s insistence on tangibility. Although the database is online, the tangible component is important. “The tangible provides an extraordinary possibility of collaborating,” Baladi says during a talk held in Diwan Bookstore on September 8, describing her attachment to sourcing materials and working with artists to produce physical installations. In the same room, there are several photographs. One of them delivers a sharp sense of doom; it’s an image of a black sea, its waves foaming, captured at night time. The rawness of the photo contrasts with the tapestry depictions, which, while still real, are more narrativized, delivering known stories and experiences the public has been exposed to in ways that try to make them comprehensible. Whereas in this photo, there is a harshness of the unknown you encounter; you are left to imagine the potential stories and experiences it holds, the different realities. It cuts through the frame and immediately into your brain. It is daunting. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. In The Anatomist, the publication launched in tandem with the exhibition as another layer of navigation that Baladi and her team propose, Rafaelle Bertault describes her experience as a migration caseworker conducting interviews and the day she decided to quit. One day, six years into working this job, she met a man with severe post-traumatic stress disorder whose friend had drowned after they tried to escape on a smuggling boat from Turkey that capsized. “He started crying and blaming himself for his death. I broke down and cried too. And so did the interpreter.” Describing it as a tipping point in the text titled Shipwreck, she writes that she was angry that all of this could have been prevented. Bertault had the same reaction six years later, in June 2023, to the news of one of the deadliest migrant disasters in history, the capsizing of the Adriana, a boat carrying 750 undocumented migrants from Libya which sank in Greek waters. Only 103 passengers survived, and the bodies of 82 people were recovered. “When I heard the journalist ask the sea-rescue activists whether the ‘migrants should have been saved’ (and it is a legal obligation to do so), I screamed,” she writes. A week later, “a French submarine was chartered at great expense to search for the five presumed dead billionaires who had each spent $25,000 to visit the site of the Titanic’s wreck. Here the journalists asked whether the rich men could be saved.” It was revealed last year that the Greek coastguard was aware of the boat in distress and chose not to intervene in the 12 hours before it capsized. Also in the publication, Jonathan Hearn reflects on the feeling of losing one’s sense of place as he describes Edge of Place, a painting by Radfan al-Mohammadi. The artwork Hearn is referring to was in response to the outbreak of the Yemeni civil war in 2014 and was produced when Mohammadi moved from Yemen to Egypt in 2016. Hearn describes meeting Mohammadi in 2023 at the Cairo Opera House where the artist explained that the girl’s glistening eyes in the artwork reflect the imagined future of the Yemeni anti-regime protesters of 2011. “Like al-Mohammadi, these men and women believed their political movement would build a better country. Yet, instead of entering that promised land, many now wrestle with the thought that they have given up home. Even if fragile and threatened, a known home may be worth more than a home that is only a mirage,” Hearn writes. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. Before we get to the second and final room of the exhibition, we walk through a corridor that Baladi made sure to activate. It was important for her to use the space as a way to “keep people in the work so they don’t run away or escape from it,” she says, describing the refuge an empty corridor can sometimes offer. Along the corridor, there are framed posters of text, including, for example, “WE ARE AS IT WERE STRANGERS TO OURSELVES.” The placement aims to reflect the migratory nature of existentialism, Baladi says, an internal process always in movement. There is also a poster with the text, “I AM MAN,” a visual reference of the 1968 Memphis sanitation workers strike in which more than 1300 Black sanitation workers marched through the streets to protest their dehumanization. When photographs of the strikes were published, the words and images captured became a global symbol for the demand for human dignity, the constituent of which is the simple statement of I AM MAN. The second room is presented as a classroom, complete with a student desk and a wall featuring the letters of the Arabic alphabet. Each of the 28 letters is accompanied by an image and a word: ب for بلد ( balad ), ت for تاريخ ( tareekh ), ث for ثورة ( thawra ), ح for حرية ( horreya ), خ for خبز ( khobz ). Country, history, revolution, freedom, bread. To the opposite wall, there is a framed poster, The Wheel, a collage bursting with revolution iconography, sourced from the internet, arranged in the shape of a circle, with what appears to be blood splattered along the top frame. And in between those two walls, a screen is installed on a chalkboard wall, playing a video introducing us to the online archive, Anatomy of Revolution. The classroom points to pedagogy as a playful mechanism in the exhibition, one which Baladi imbues with her own references, including from the online archive. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. Returning to the point of entry, adjacent to the For the Glory of the Wind and Water tapestry, a quote from French philosopher Gilles Deleuze is arranged on the wall in the shape of a zigzag. “Z is for zig zag. The fly, the zed of the fly, the rigging movements of the fly, the Zed. It is the final word. There is no word after zigzag. […] It is perhaps the elementary movement, Z as movement, the fly…perhaps the movement that presided at the creation of the world.” Deleuze is also featured in The Anatomist’s How to Read a Dictionary According to Deleuze. In the text, Farida Youssef, who co-edited the publication with Baladi, argues for Deleuze’s Z for zigzag concept in reading a dictionary: to reorient our ways of thinking by moving from the traditional approach of reading from cover to cover, in a way in which the rigid, linear sequence of the alphabet determines the order of comprehension, a predetermined structure set in stone, and to instead navigate such a book like a zigzag, in an agile practice offering other possibilities for the development of ideas, linkages and potentials. This turns reading into a dynamic, physical process of concept creation, of flying in a zigzag from place to place to trace connections and form knowledge. “If you start with ‘c for colonialism’ and then read ‘w for war’ before ending with ‘m for migration,’ you will probably understand the concept of ‘i for injustice’,” Youssef writes. In the exhibition, the placement and dispersal of the items throughout the room, whether on the wall, in a frame, on a table, and their relation to one another forces the navigating viewer, as well as their attention, into an anatomical movement, reminiscent of the zigzag, a disruptive, disorienting but logical interruption to a traditional, simpler or predetermined flow. The same applies in terms of the exhibition’s other modes to navigate, the publication and website, and in how they relate to each other as well as to the other physical elements, engaging the participant into a referential dance of a similar nature. The choice of the words of Deleuze and the figures of the zigzag are suited to the aspiration behind the publication. In L’Abécédaire de Gilles Deleuze , a series of interviews published posthumously, Deleuze explains to journalist Claire Parnet his theory on the zigzag. “It’s the Zed of bifurcation, of lightning,” he tells her, “and a great letter that establishes a return to A.” Speaking in terms of physics , he discusses how to bring divergent singularities, or different potentials, into relation with one another. According to him, a phenomenon occurs between two potentials through a “somber precursor.” Once that precursor situation begins, the potentials are left in a state of reaction from which a visible event emerges. “So, there is the somber precursor and then a lightning bolt, and that’s how the world was born. There is always a somber precursor that no one sees and then the lightning bolt that illuminates, and there is the world,” he says. Baladi refers to the zigzag as a methodology for the exhibition. No one can dispute the sight of a bolt of lightning. It is undeniable. The exhibition is a collation and exploration of these bolts and the moments which preceded them, the somber precursors that have led to a certain state of reaction. Seen in this light, the bolts engage a piercing public and intimate understanding of a struggle for freedom, an undeniable recognition of what became a symbol, born out of this zap of conception. Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. But what happens when this mode of navigation is presented to a public to whom symbols are to be interpreted and connections to be made, as individuals and, also, collectively? Aside from the works on exhibit, the written work, which steers interpretation into a discourse, the website and the overall philosophy of the zigzag, there is much left in the hands of the audience. They exist as participants in the practice of protecting and engaging with knowledge and, specifically, the visual identities of history, by seeking to understand or collectively remember what is being displayed. The exhibition, with the website as its umbrella, asks us to reflect on images and symbols that have garnered a mass social response at a certain time. For example, if we scroll down to “ت” or “Ta,” we find an entry for torture. Among the data compiled in the section, there are images from the Iranian Woman, Life, Freedom uprising, which was triggered by the killing of Mahsa Amini after she was arrested by Iranian morality police in 2022. Below the social media artwork, there is a collage of the mugshots of women who were tortured at the Towhid Prison run by Iran’s pre-revolution intelligence service, SAVAK, which was overseen by the shah from 1957-1979, accompanied by a quote: “Torture still scars Iranians 40 years after revolution,” originally published in The San Francisco Chronicle by Nasser Karimi and Job Gambrell. Both are installed at the prison’s premises in Tehran, which now operates instead as the Ebrat museum of torture. When asked about the shift in the exhibition’s modes of viewing, its intention to traverse from individual to the collective, the personal and the public, one visitor speaks of the fragmentary air of the project that, in a way, dismantles collective experiences into moments, fragments and details, summoning a different kind of attention than what is wielded when remembering something collectively. “It’s like the exhibition dismantles the public of revolution, alongside revolution itself, breaking their wholeness open, maybe for a possible re-arrangement or just running with one of the fragments. It’s an interesting license the artist and the art take for themselves. It’s almost a license to disorient us, despite the dictionary, the database and all these pedagogic gestures. And we aren’t disoriented together. We are disoriented alone, facing what is being done to a memory once collective. The only collective experience is that we are just a bunch of merry exhibition goers and art consumers,” they say. In Baladi’s own narrative, voiced during the September talk in Diwan, she responds on the relation: “Revolution, the dirty word. … This is not about revolution. It’s about what happens after.” Her question is, ultimately, how art addresses revolution. It is about how symbols are taken, used, interpreted and reinterpreted, or reformed, she says. The above visitor wonders, “What does this intention make of art?” Courtesy of the artist and Gypsum. Photo by Marc Onsi. The journey of Zarafa is a promise of a life unrealized, masked under the cover of diplomacy. Baladi was initiating the Anatomy of Revolution project in 2019 when she added Zarafa’s story, with a quest to investigate questions of cultural exchange. This shows up elsewhere in the exhibition. In the middle of the first room, we see a stuffed panda sitting in a transparent box, a reference to Chinese Panda diplomacy, when China used to offer pandas as diplomatic gifts until the practice was stopped in the 1980s. The panda has its back to the corridor which leads to the classroom part of the exhibition. In the same room, there are also references of diplomatic exchange and political persuasion, including a “cabinet of curiosities” with objects referring to ceremonial gifts exchanged between state heads, as well as ceramic objects displayed on tables referencing pharaonic medallions, a symbol for military achievement. In migration, a physical and psychological process, surviving is for the lucky ones. But in being granted the privilege of continuation, what does life look like then? Is it a life of our choosing? Or are we captive, physically, psychologically, to the limits constricting us, which, if we’re not careful, will determine how we think, what we think or if we even think at all? What we risk is having a pacifying but fake, implanted, shared meaning, engineering a collective identity designed to produce a mechanical mass social behavior and response. All of this has led me to thinking of revolution as a journey distorted, one archived in life, deformed or buried alive, in most cases; prematurely fossilized, or captured, and frozen in time. And so, Zarafa’s life, maybe, is also a metaphor for revolution. A story holding the painful movement to another place for the promise of a certain freedom, driven and shaped by politics. And we are left to think about what happens when we arrive, post-movement. What becomes of the memory, and how do we remember? The post ‘Revolution, the dirty word’: On Lara Baladi’s Z for Zarafa first appeared on Mada Masr .

items.title: Cancer du sein et du col de l’utérus : AGEROUTE Guinée mise sur la sensibilisation pour sauver des vies
items.description: Face aux ravages du cancer du sein et du col de l’utérus, AGEROUTE Guinée fait de la sensibilisation un levier de prévention et de protection de la santé des femmes. A travers une séance d’information animée par des spécialistes en gynécologie-obstétrique, les travailleurs de l’institution ont été édifiés sur les causes, les signes d’alerte, l’importance du dépistage précoce et les conséquences d’une prise en charge tardive. Une initiative qui a suscité une prise de conscience et fait naître un engagement collectif : relayer l’information pour sauver des vies. Briser le silence, lever les tabous et encourager les femmes à se faire dépister, c’est le message fort qui a marqué la séance de sensibilisation organisée par l’Agence de gestion des routes de Guinée (AGEROUTE Guinée) autour du cancer du sein et du col de l’utérus. Dans une société où le manque d’information, la gêne et la peur peuvent encore retarder le recours aux soins, cette initiative s’inscrit dans une démarche de prévention et de responsabilisation face à des maladies dont les conséquences peuvent être dramatiques lorsqu’elles sont détectées tardivement. Au cœur des échanges, Dr Havanatou Camara, gynécologue-obstétricienne à la retraite, a délivré un message sans équivoque : le dépistage précoce constitue une étape essentielle pour détecter les lésions précancéreuses, identifier les cancers à un stade précoce et améliorer les chances de traitement. Avec des mots simples, mais empreints d’une profonde conviction, la spécialiste a invité les femmes à ne pas attendre l’apparition de symptômes graves avant de consulter. « Toutes les femmes à partir de 25 ans doivent aller dans une structure où l’on peut faire le dépistage du cancer du col », a-t-elle recommandé, en insistant sur l’importance d’une prise en charge rapide lorsque les résultats révèlent une anomalie. Pour elle, la lutte contre le cancer du col de l’utérus exige avant tout une mobilisation collective, une meilleure connaissance des moyens de prévention et un accès effectif aux services de dépistage et de soins. Son intervention a également été marquée par un appel à dépasser la gêne et les préjugés qui éloignent encore certaines femmes des structures sanitaires. « Ne vous gênez pas, ne vous découragez pas », a-t-elle lancé, encourageant les participantes à se tourner vers des professionnels qualifiés, capables de les accompagner dans le dépistage et, si nécessaire, dans la prise en charge médicale. La gynécologue-obstétricienne a par ailleurs salué l’initiative de la direction générale d’AGEROUTE Guinée, qu’elle considère comme une occasion importante de rapprocher l’information sanitaire des travailleuses et travailleurs. Au-delà du cadre professionnel, elle souhaite voir ce type de sensibilisation toucher un public plus large, afin que les connaissances acquises deviennent un véritable outil de prévention au sein des familles et des communautés. A l’issue de cette rencontre, Malick Bangoura, chef du service juridique et contentieux à AGEROUTE Guinée, s’est réjoui de la qualité des enseignements reçus. Au nom de cette volonté de faire de la prévention une responsabilité partagée, il a salué l’initiative de la direction générale, qui a permis aux participants de mieux comprendre les causes du cancer du sein et du col de l’utérus, les mesures de prévention ainsi que les conséquences d’un défaut de prise en charge à temps. Pour lui, la satisfaction exprimée à l’issue de la séance doit désormais se traduire par des actions concrètes. Dans un contexte où l’information peut contribuer à sauver des vies, chaque participant est appelé à devenir un relais auprès de ses proches, de ses connaissances et de son entourage. Il a ainsi plaidé pour la multiplication de telles initiatives, tout en évoquant la nécessité d’approfondir la réflexion sur la question et d’encourager une contribution accrue du secteur privé aux efforts de prévention. Cette volonté de transmettre l’information trouve un écho particulier chez Aïcha Condé, chargée de projets à AGEROUTE Guinée. Marquée par les explications de Dr Havanatou Camara, elle reconnaît avoir pris davantage conscience des dangers liés à ces maladies et de l’importance du dépistage, y compris chez les femmes instruites. « Je suis sûre que je vais aller directement au centre de dépistage », confie-t-elle, déterminée à mettre en pratique les enseignements reçus. Son témoignage traduit l’un des objectifs majeurs de la rencontre : transformer la sensibilisation en une décision personnelle, puis cette décision en un réflexe durable de prévention. Consciente des réalités sociales et familiales auxquelles de nombreuses femmes sont confrontées, Aïcha Condé souhaite également porter ce message au-delà de son lieu de travail. Elle exhorte les femmes de Guinée à dépasser leurs appréhensions et à faire de leur santé une priorité. Pour elle, le dépistage ne doit être ni une source de honte ni une démarche que l’on repousse à plus tard, mais un acte de responsabilité envers soi-même et sa famille. Le même sentiment de prise de conscience anime Margueritte Loua, stagiaire à la Direction administrative et des ressources humaines d’AGEROUTE Guinée. Si le cancer est une maladie dont elle avait déjà entendu parler, les explications détaillées sur ses manifestations et ses conséquences lui ont permis de mieux mesurer les risques et l’importance d’une vigilance accrue. Elle retient notamment qu’il ne faut pas attendre que la maladie se manifeste à un stade avancé pour agir. Son appel à effectuer des examens de dépistage résume l’esprit de cette rencontre : mieux connaître la maladie pour mieux la prévenir, et diffuser les informations essentielles afin de protéger les personnes exposées. En ouvrant ses portes à cette initiative de sensibilisation, AGEROUTE Guinée rappelle ainsi que la responsabilité d’une institution ne se limite pas à ses missions professionnelles. Elle peut aussi s’exprimer à travers des actions qui contribuent au bien-être de son personnel et à la diffusion de messages d’intérêt public. Au terme de cette rencontre, les participants repartent avec des connaissances renforcées, mais surtout avec un engagement : faire circuler l’information et encourager les femmes à franchir le pas du dépistage. Car face au cancer, le silence et l’attente peuvent coûter cher, tandis que l’information, la prévention et une prise en charge précoce peuvent faire toute la différence. A AGEROUTE Guinée, le message est désormais clair : se faire dépister, c’est agir à temps ; sensibiliser, c’est contribuer à sauver des vies.

items.title: Fuite de données au Grand Orient de France : des documents nominatifs et financiers exposés
items.description: La secte maconnique, qui revendique plus de 50 000 membres et environ 1 400 loges, a confirme, jeudi 15 octobre, avoir constate la circulation de fichiers qui lui sont attribues, tout en assurant que ses systemes d'information centraux n'ont pas ete compromis. Des centaines de fichiers internes mis en ligne Selon le site FrenchBreaches, specialise dans les fuites de donnees, l'ensemble documentaire comprend 737 fichiers, dont 727 PDF totalisant plus de 9 000 pages. Ces documents, qui datent principalement de 2017 a 2026, incluent des communiques, des discours, des circulaires, des comptes rendus de reunions du Conseil de l'Ordre, des budgets et des rapports financiers. Plus sensible, un tableau nominatif de septembre 2024 contient des noms, prenoms, adresses e-mail et numeros de telephone associes a une loge. Dans un communique, le Grand Orient de France a precise : « Les verifications techniques etablissent que les systemes d'information centraux de l'obedience, proteges par une double authentification, n'ont pas ete compromis. Une part importante des fichiers diffuses correspond a des documents non sensibles. » Des documents attribués au Grand Orient de France circulent. L’Obédience a porté plainte, une enquête est en cours. Nos systèmes centraux n'ont pas été compromis et les données sensibles ont été protégées grâce à une sécurité renforcée. https://t.co/X4EtsA68gx — GODF (Officiel) (@GODFOfficiel) October 15, 2026 L'institution, tres active lors du vote de la loi sur l'euthanasie , a toutefois depose plainte, et une enquete est en cours. La diffusion a ete revendiquee par les groupes LunarisSec et Akatsuki Cyber Team. Dans un message publie sur un forum cybercriminel, le responsable de ce dernier presente l'operation comme un « avertissement » motive par des « incidents lies a l'islam » et des critiques a l'egard du salafisme, sans que le lien avec l'obedience soit clairement etabli. La provenance de cette cyberattaque contre la secte maconnique, qui reserve generalement ses critiques a l'eglise catholique, est etonnante.

items.title: Recours du Hafia FC devant le TAS : le Tribunal Arbitral du Sport ordonne le report de la confrontation AS Douanes – CR Belouizdad demandé par le Hafia FC
items.description: Le Hafia Football Club informe ses supporters, ses partenaires et l'opinion sportive que le Tribunal Arbitral du Sport (TAS), saisi de son recours contre la décision de la Confédération Africaine de Football (CAF) de faire rejouer le match retour du premier tour préliminaire de la Coupe de la Confédération CAF 2026/2027 contre l'AS Douanes (Mauritanie), a rendu ce vendredi 16 octobre 2026 une ordonnance de mesures provisionnelles dans l'affaire TAS 2026/A/12858. Après examen de la requête du Hafia FC, le TAS a ordonné à la CAF de reporter la double confrontation du deuxième tour préliminaire opposant l'AS Douanes au CR Belouizdad (Algérie), initialement prévue le 17 octobre 2026 (aller) et du 23 au 25 octobre 2026 (retour). Le Tribunal a notamment relevé que la décision de la CAF retenant la force majeure ne comportait aucune motivation, et que l'appel interne du club devant le Jury d'Appel de la CAF, introduit dès le 16 septembre 2026, était resté sans réponse. Cette ordonnance constitue une victoire importante pour le Hafia FC. Elle préserve pleinement les droits du club dans la suite de la procédure et garantit qu'une décision favorable au fond ne sera pas privée d'effet par un fait accompli sportif. Le Hafia FC maintient sa contestation d'une décision de la CAF qu'il estime non fondée, la non-présentation de l'AS Douanes à Conakry le 11 septembre 2026 relevant selon lui de défaillances organisationnelles évitables et non d'un cas de force majeure. La procédure au fond se poursuit devant le TAS. Le Hafia FC tiendra le public informé de chaque nouvelle étape et remercie ses supporters pour leur soutien constant et leur patience. La Direction du Hafia Football Club

items.title: PM Shehbaz reaffirms support for Saudi Arabia in meeting with new envoy
items.description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday reaffirmed Pakistan’s support for Saudi Arabia in safeguarding its “sovereignty, security and territorial integrity” amid a recent escalation in Houthi attacks. According to a statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO), the premier made the remarks during a meeting with newly appointed Saudi Ambassador Dr Rajeh Tami Albugamy. He welcomed the envoy to Pakistan and congratulated him on assuming his new responsibilities. Ambassador Albugamy, assumed his diplomatic responsibilities in Islamabad on Thursday, reaffirming the commitment to strengthening the strategic and fraternal ties between the two countries. During the meeting, PM Shehbaz said Pakistan-Saudi Arabia relations had made significant progress in recent years and reaffirmed Islamabad’s commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation across various sectors. He “strongly condemned” the recent escalation in Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, which had resulted in deaths and injuries, including among Pakistani nationals, the statement said. The prime minister also said the two countries had always stood by each other, adding that the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement and the Makkah Joint Defence Alliance marked “historic milestones” in their longstanding fraternal relations and reflected their shared commitment to regional peace and security. PM Shehbaz also thanked the Saudi leadership for its longstanding economic and financial support to Pakistan and assured the ambassador of Pakistan’s full support and cooperation in further strengthening bilateral ties. Ambassador Albugamy also met Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, where the latter underscored longstanding fraternal and strategic ties between Islamabad and Riyadh, according to the Foreign Office (FO). He also reaffirmed Pakistan and Saudi Arabia’s “shared commitment to further strengthen bilateral cooperation for mutual progress and prosperity”. The FO added that the new Saudi envoy conveyed greetings from the kingdom’s leadership to Pakistan, with Dar reciprocating and conveying his best wishes to Saudi King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and other Saudi leaders. The meeting comes amid heightened tensions in the Middle East. On Wednesday, Yemen’s Houthi rebels said they had targeted facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco, after Saudi officials reported a strike on a building in Riyadh housing the energy giant’s operations centre. Powerful explosions also rattled the Saudi capital, as the coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted a missile fired by the group towards Riyadh. On Tuesday, Saudi Arabia launched strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen, targeting fuel and energy facilities it said were being used to support missile and drone attacks, as the Yemeni group threatened a “harsh and painful” response against Saudi airports, refineries and oil installations. Hours later, Saudi authorities issued warnings of potential hostile aerial threats in the kingdom’s eastern province and Riyadh. Loud explosions were heard near Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran, according to witnesses. Later, a Saudi energy ministry official confirmed the attack. Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency said that four people — two women, a man and a child — were wounded by debris from two intercepted Houthi cruise missiles in the capital and that 15 homes were damaged. The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s coalition government unravelled in July. Against this backdrop, Pakistan has repeatedly expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia. On October 5, in an emergency meeting of the Makkah pact in Riyadh, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye agreed to the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who was part of Pakistan’s delegation in the meeting, maintained that Pakistan and Turkiye had “presence in theatre” and only Saudi troops were involved in combat operations. On September 18, Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Pakistan would go to “any extent” to defend the Gulf state, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”. Asif has also reaffirmed that Pakistan will “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalates. The defence minister said that Pakistan would fulfil all its obligations under the Makkah Defence Alliance in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the three countries. At the same time, Pakistan has also asserted that the alliance is intended for collective deterrence and is defensive in nature.

items.title: Government secures financing to fix water shortages in Tamale, Yendi and Damongo
items.description: Finance Minister Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson has announced a €323 million financing package for the Northern Ghana Water and Sanitation Project, aimed at addressing persistent water shortages in Tamale, Yendi and Damongo. The package comprises €98 million in grants and a €225 million highly concessional facility from the European Investment Bank (EIB). Dr. Forson outlined the financing following a meeting with EIB Vice-President Ambroise Fayolle, describing the discussions as productive. “I have just concluded a productive meeting with European Investment Bank Vice-President Ambroise Fayolle on the financing package for the Northern Ghana Water and Sanitation Project,” he said. The European Commission will provide a €68 million grant, while Invest International, the Dutch government initiative, will contribute a further €30 million grant. The EIB’s highly concessional facility accounts for the remaining €225 million. According to the Finance Minister, the project will address recurring water shortages and improve sanitation across the three communities.

items.title: Contrôle des prix: deux caves et cinq maquis ont été scellés dans le Bankui
items.description: (Pâ, le 16 octobre 2026) Du 8 au 14 octobre 2026, la Direction régionale de l’Industrie, du Commerce et de l’Artisanat du Bankui (DRICA-BNK) a mené une vaste opération de contrôle des prix à Poura et à Pa. Au total, 275 points de vente ont été inspectés afin de lutter contre les pratiques spéculatives sur les produits de grande consommation et de veiller au respect de la réglementation commerciale. Cette opération a permis de constater des manquements liés à la vente de bière au-delà des tarifs réglementaires. En conséquence, deux caves et cinq maquis ont été scellés. Les commerçants concernés ont également fait l’objet de sanctions. À travers cette opération, la DRICA-BNK rappelle qu’aucune augmentation des prix de la bière n’a été décidée. Elle invite les tenanciers de caves et de maquis à respecter strictement les tarifs en vigueur, sous peine de sanctions conformément à la réglementation. La DRICA-BNK réaffirme ainsi sa vigilance dans la lutte contre les pratiques commerciales illicites et appelle les acteurs du commerce à faire preuve de responsabilité afin de préserver les intérêts des consommateurs. items.title: Le Maroc désigné deuxième vice-président du G-24
items.description: Le Royaume assurera la deuxième vice-présidence du G-24 à partir du 1er novembre 2026, avant d’accéder à la première vice-présidence en 2027, puis à la présidence du groupe en 2028. Cette désignation renforce son rôle dans les discussions internationales sur les enjeux monétaires et financiers. Le Maroc a été désigné pour assurer la deuxième vice-présidence du G-24, un groupe intergouvernemental qui coordonne les positions des pays en développement sur les questions monétaires et financières internationales. Cette responsabilité prendra effet le 1er novembre 2026, à l’issue de la réunion ministérielle annuelle du Groupe, tenue à Bangkok en marge des Assemblées annuelles du Fonds monétaire international (FMI) et de la Banque mondiale. Selon le mécanisme de rotation des responsabilités au sein du G-24, le Royaume devrait accéder à la première vice-présidence en 2027, puis à la présidence en 2028. Cette évolution témoigne de la confiance accordée au Maroc par les pays membres et de son engagement en faveur du renforcement de la coopération économique et financière internationale. À cette occasion, le Royaume a réaffirmé sa volonté de contribuer à la cohésion du Groupe, de défendre les priorités des économies émergentes et en développement et de promouvoir une architecture monétaire et financière internationale plus représentative, plus réactive et plus équitable. Le Maroc entend également favoriser le dialogue entre les pays membres, encourager la recherche de consensus et participer à l’élaboration de propositions concrètes face aux défis économiques et financiers communs. Des enjeux économiques mondiaux au cœur des discussions La réunion ministérielle annuelle du G-24 a été présidée par le ministre des Finances du Nigeria, Taiwo Oyedele. Elle a notamment enregistré la participation de la directrice générale du FMI, Kristalina Georgieva, ainsi que du directeur général et directeur des connaissances du Groupe de la Banque mondiale, Paschal Donohoe. Les échanges ont porté sur plusieurs défis majeurs auxquels l’économie mondiale est confrontée, notamment les incertitudes économiques, les tensions géopolitiques, la fragmentation des échanges et le durcissement des conditions de financement. Les participants ont souligné la nécessité de renforcer la coopération internationale afin de préserver la stabilité macroéconomique et de soutenir la croissance des pays émergents et en développement, dans un contexte marqué par des contraintes financières persistantes. La délégation marocaine, composée de représentants du ministère de l’Économie et des Finances, de Bank Al-Maghrib et des représentations du Royaume auprès du FMI et de la Banque mondiale, a pris part à ces discussions. À travers cette nouvelle responsabilité, le Maroc sera appelé à contribuer davantage à la coordination des positions des pays en développement et aux réflexions sur l’évolution du système monétaire et financier international. The post Le Maroc désigné deuxième vice-président du G-24 appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: He Joined the Military. They Reported His Wife to ICE.
items.description: G iovanna Perez loaded her four kids into the car on September 21 and drove from their home in Weslaco, Texas, to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. She had a 9:30 a.m. appointment to pick up the ID cards that would allow them to access military medical insurance, facilities, and commissary stores. Her husband, Pedro Gutierrez, had recently enlisted in the Army and left a month earlier for basic training at Fort Benning, in Georgia. Perez approached the military guards at the gates with some trepidation. Her parents illegally brought her across the U.S. border from Mexico when she was 6 years old. Now 35, she and Gutierrez have been together since they were 17 and have carefully kept her immigration status a secret. Gutierrez is a U.S. citizen, but marriage does not give legal status to someone who is in the country unlawfully. When the Obama administration started the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program to protect immigrants like Perez who had arrived as children, she did not apply, for fear that the government might someday use the information against her family. Perez told us that her husband believed that joining the Army would allow him to serve his country, give his family access to health care—including the costly medications his son takes—and potentially protect his wife from deportation. He had already submitted her application for a benefit called Parole in Place, which offers a path to legal residency for the close relatives of service members. Officials at Fort Benning had assured him that she would have no trouble getting IDs for herself and the children, and that it didn’t matter that she didn’t have a Social Security number, Perez told us. At the gates of the Navy base, guards told Perez they had no record of her appointment. She remained calm as they directed her to a nearby office to get a visitor’s pass. That’s when two military officials took the family into a room for questioning. “In my head, I thought it was just protocol for the safety of the base, but it started getting weird,” Perez said. As she answered, she told us, one of the military officers appeared to be relaying her responses to someone through text messages. Two other men entered the room. They wore khaki pants, she said, not military fatigues. The patches on their shirts said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement . It appeared to Perez that they’d been waiting for her, at the base or somewhere nearby. The men told Perez to report to the ICE office in Harlingen, Texas, in three days. Her older children, ages 17, 15, and 11, were confused. “My kids were just, like, What’s going on? ” Perez told us. “ Are they gonna detain you? Why are they doing this to us? I thought you were supposed to be safe. ” Perez didn’t know what to tell them, and she had no way to call her husband. When she went to the ICE office three days later, she was booked and issued an order to appear in immigration court. She suspected the military shared her information with ICE. And now the government was trying to deport her. P erez’s attorney, Alex Martinez , told us he’s trying to determine whether other families have been targeted in similar ways. He suspects that the government has been using Parole in Place to gather information for immigration-enforcement purposes—the opposite of what military recruits are led to believe. “There’s no bigger betrayal to our soldiers than to use their trust in a program, set out by our government to protect their families, and ultimately use it to destroy their families while they’re serving our country and putting their lives on the line,” Martinez told us. “You’re stabbing your own soldiers in the back.” Gabriel V. Cárdenas for The Atlantic Perez shows a photo of her husband, who is at military training. The Associated Press in August identified at least 50 cases in which close family of active-duty service members were arrested by ICE. What’s different about Perez’s case is that U.S. military personnel appeared to be working with ICE to identify a potential target and use a long-standing military-recruitment tool—the promise of legal status for loved ones—to facilitate an arrest. ICE confirmed to us in a statement that Navy personnel had reported Perez to immigration officers when the family arrived at the base. The Department of Homeland Security and ICE “value the contributions of all those who serve in the U.S. military,” the statement said. “Having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation’s laws. Military service by an immediate relative does not automatically grant parole, lawful status, or immunity from immigration enforcement." Perez told us the ICE officers seemed to be expecting her, told her they knew that Gutierrez had applied for Parole in Place, and asked questions about a trip her son had taken with his grandmother to Mexico years earlier. Neither the Army nor the Office of the Secretary of Defense responded to requests for comment, but one defense official told us that there have been “varying degrees of cooperation between military installations and the Department of Homeland Security” for more than a year. The official declined to be named because he, like others we spoke with, was not authorized to talk publicly about this issue. Another official told us that DHS often made such requests to installations at a local level, but there were inconsistent degrees of cooperation. The Navy declined to comment. [ Read: Trump loves ICE. Its workforce has never been so miserable. ] Within months of President Trump’s second inauguration, military mental-health specialists began telling us that service members within their units were fearful about how the administration’s crackdown on immigrants could affect their families. They described spouses afraid to go on base while their partner was deployed, family members too scared to leave their home, and uniformed service members accompanying loved ones to immigration appointments or hearings with the hope that their presence would make immigration officials or judges pause. Such worries, the specialists said, were becoming a distraction for those serving, particularly during deployments. It was an early sign of a break in a long-standing bargain: A government that asks Americans to take extraordinary risks would not add stress that could distract service members from their missions. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth frequently touts the military’s surging recruitment numbers. Less often mentioned is the military’s success in recruiting from some of the country’s most heavily Hispanic communities, including the Rio Grande Valley of South Texas, where Perez and Gutierrez live. Hispanic recruits accounted for nearly 27 percent of new Army soldiers last year, up from just less than 20 percent in 2020, according to Army statistics. This population remains key to the Army meeting its recruiting standards even as service members from these communities have reported that their families have been targeted by ICE. M ilitary law enforcement cannot provide direct support to civilian law enforcement, under the Posse Comitatus Act, a 19th-century law that was intended to keep the military from meddling in the affairs of southern states. But to secure an installation, military police can inspect those who enter. “Anytime somebody makes an appointment on a military base, that information could get shared throughout the federal government,” Margaret D. Stock, an immigration lawyer and former Army Reserve officer who helped develop the Military Accessions Vital to the National Interest (MAVNI) program, told us. Under the Trump administration, those who serve, along with their families, are no more protected from immigration enforcement than those submitting their data to any other government agency. “The military is no longer immune from this,” Stock said. Some troops are asking for overseas assignments where they can live with their family members, far from ICE agents. In April, ICE officers arrested the 22-year-old wife of a U.S. soldier when the couple moved to an Army base in Louisiana. The woman, Annie Ramos, was born in Honduras and had a previous deportation order issued in absentia when she was a toddler. Ramos was released after Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona, a Democrat, spoke with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on her behalf. Bobby Pulido, a Democratic candidate in the Rio Grande Valley who is running for Congress, has cited her case as an example of ICE overreach by the Trump administration. “The scary part is they’re doubling down on it. They don’t care,” Pulido said in a video clip with Perez that his campaign posted on social media on Wednesday. It used to be that the military was seen as a potential pathway to U.S. citizenship. Military service can qualify noncitizens for expedited naturalization, and the Pentagon has at times recruited people who were not permanent residents. More than 180,000 members of the U.S. military have become naturalized citizens since 2002, according to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. In 2008, at the height of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, the Pentagon launched the MAVNI program, which allowed some immigrants who were living legally in the U.S. but were not citizens to enlist based on specialized skills considered vital, including medical expertise and foreign-language proficiency. The program expired in 2017 and was not renewed. The government established the Parole in Place benefit in 2010, allowing family members to remain in the United States and apply for legal status. Approval is discretionary and does not guarantee a green card. But the promise remains a powerful recruiting tool for the armed services in immigrant communities. [ Read: The northern passage ] Perez said she has no criminal record and no previous deportation orders. She met her husband at a quinceañera party when they were teenagers in Laredo. Gutierrez drove commercial trucks but decided to enlist in the Army to secure health-insurance coverage for the family and college-tuition aid for their older children. Fixing Perez’s immigration status was another incentive for him, she told us. Gabriel V. Cárdenas for The Atlantic Perez plays with her 2-year-old son at their home in Weslaco, Texas. It was in a 20-minute weekend phone call that Gutierrez learned the country he was serving had been trying to deport his wife and separate his family . Had Perez been sent to a detention center, as many immigrants are, Gutierrez would have been forced to leave basic training to care for his children—a governmental loss of not just a new service member but also roughly $50,000 in sunk training costs, according to Army estimates. Perez stays home to take care of their 2-year-old, and she told us she has no idea what would happen to her children if ICE sent her to Mexico. “I have no one,” she said. “I’m by myself.” Her husband will graduate from basic training on November 5, and Perez and her children plan to drive to Georgia for the ceremony at Fort Benning. They were issued their military IDs, so they should be allowed onto the base. Perez told us that she’s in a discussion group with other military families who are asking a lot of questions about who will be allowed to attend the graduation. Five days after the ceremony, Perez will be due back in court in Texas.

items.title: FO condemns Indian minister’s ‘provocative’ remarks threatening aggression against Pakistan
items.description: The Foreign Office (FO) on Friday condemned Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh’s “provocative remarks” threatening aggression against Pakistan, saying such statements highlighting the neighbouring country’s “hegemonistic mindset”. Singh on Thursday had warned Pakistan that any “fresh terrorist activity from across the border would invite a strike even bigger than the last time”, according to Indian news agency ANI . On Friday, FO spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan was asked about the comments during his weekly press briefing. “Pakistan rejects and condemns the Indian defence minister’s provocative remarks entailing a threat of Indian aggression against Pakistan. Such reckless statements reflect India’s hegemonistic mindset and the risk its belligerent posture poses to regional peace and stability in South Asia,” he said. “We wish to remind India of the consequences of its military aggression in May last year, when Pakistan demonstrated both its capability and resolve to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and gave a befitting response and reply to Indian aggression,” he said, referring to the brief military conflict between the two countries. He said that there should be “no ambiguity” that Pakistan remained fully prepared to safeguard its “sovereignty and territorial integrity” against any “ill-advised aggression”. Haider said Pakistan’s “restraint and commitment to peace” should not be mistaken for weakness, warning that any aggression would be met with a “forceful response”. “India should draw an appropriate lesson from last year’s experience and abandon its belligerent posture and dangerous rhetoric and act with responsibility for lasting peace in the region,” he said. During the briefing, the FO spokesperson was also asked about China’s comments regarding India’s move to recognise and standardise the names of 28 geographical features in Ladakh, a disputed territory claimed by India. China had opposed the move, terming it “illegal”. The spokesperson was asked about the development in the context of the Jammu and Kashmir dispute. Khan said that said India’s actions on Aug 5, 2019 , which revoked the special autonomy of occupied Kashmir, were “illegal and void”. He added that the move could not alter the fact that Jammu and Kashmir was an internationally recognised disputed territory whose final status must be determined in accordance with relevant UN Security Council resolutions and the wishes of the Kashmiri people. Digitisation of attestation services During the press briefing, the FO spokesperson was also asked about the reforms introduced to the ministry’s attestation and apostille services. Last month, the Federal Investigation Agency’s Anti-Corruption Circle Islamabad had busted a network allegedly involved in the preparation and use of fake apostille stickers in connivance with officials from the foreign ministry. Khan said on Friday that the foreign ministry was progressively digitising and automating apostille services to make them faster, more transparent and accessible. He said that e-attestation had been launched through the ministry’s portal, while the transition to e-apostille services was under way. He added that eligible applicants could be exempted from “physical appearances, subject to prescribed safeguards”, a move that would particularly facilitate overseas Pakistanis. “This is a massive leap forward,” he said, adding that the process was ongoing and Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar had personally steered the initiative. He said that an inquiry into irregularities regarding the services was underway and the results would be announced when it was completed.

items.title: Watching for a Blue Wave in South Carolina
items.description: Nancy Lacore found out she was fired as the chief of the Navy Reserve almost a year to the day after she got the job. On a Friday morning in August 2025, Admiral James Kilby, then the acting chief of naval operations, called Lacore to his office in the Pentagon. She went alone, and when she asked how Kilby was doing, his reply—“Not good”—told her all she needed to know. By the time Kilby delivered the news, he had tears in his eyes, Lacore says. He told her that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had directed him to relieve her of command effective immediately. No reason was given. “I kind of fell forward a little bit on the table,” Lacore told me. “It just knocked the wind out of me for a second.” Lacore is among the dozens of military leaders that Hegseth has sacked or ousted over the past year and a half, many of them women and people of color. She’s since taken a different path: Lacore recounted her story to me after a campaign event outside Charleston, South Carolina, where she is asking voters to send her back to Washington—this time as a member of Congress. When Lacore left the Pentagon on that summer Friday, she never returned, her 35-year military career effectively over. (The Pentagon declined to comment.) By January, she had launched a bid as a Democrat for the House in South Carolina’s Low Country. South Carolina’s First District is a reach for Democrats, but it is one of more than a dozen races across the country where the party is testing how deep into GOP territory it can advance in November. President Trump carried the district by 13 points in 2024. Democrats flipped the seat in 2018, during their blue midterm wave in Trump’s first term. But Republicans won it back two years later and then redrew the district’s lines to cement their advantage. Now the unpopularity of both Trump and the outgoing incumbent, Representative Nancy Mace, has put the seat in play again for Democrats. (Mace ran for governor—she lost badly in the primary—instead of for reelection to the House.) Democrats see Lacore’s long military record, moderate policy positions, and steady demeanor as an ideal fit for a constituency that is more country-club Republican than MAGA, and which seems to have grown exhausted by the headline-grabbing Mace. Indeed, most of the political operatives I spoke with said Lacore would probably be in an even better position if Mace were her opponent; instead, she is facing Jenny Costa Honeycutt, a Republican Charleston County council member who is distancing herself from Mace by pledging to steer clear of “clickbait politics.” Lacore is a former Republican who left the party during Trump’s first presidential run. Like many other Democratic candidates this year, she has placed affordability at the center of her platform. She talks about her experience as a mother of six kids as much as her decades in the Navy, and the challenges she faced juggling a large family in which both she and her husband were service members, and overseas deployments seem to resonate in a district with a large military presence. During a veterans’ forum I attended, Lacore’s call to end the Iran war drew hearty applause. Although Lacore mentions her firing by Hegseth on the campaign trail, she’s not trying to portray herself as a “resistance” hero. (Such candidacies have not fared particularly well .) She pitches herself as a supporter of border security and law enforcement; one of her daughters, she notes, is a police officer. When I asked Lacore where she parted ways with the national Democratic Party, she took the opportunity to distance herself from the far left: “I am not a socialist,” she replied. “They can’t really hang a lot of the woke stuff on her or try to make her out to be some sort of weirdo,” Ed Sutton, a Democratic state senator in the area, told me. Without a long political record to scrutinize, Republicans have harped on Lacore’s thin ties to the district; she bought a home in the Charleston area only last year, having planned to retire there at the end of her four-year term as Navy Reserve chief (which Hegseth cut short). During a debate last Wednesday, Honeycutt took every opportunity to remind viewers that Lacore had been, until recently, an out-of-towner. Lacore’s Democratic-primary opponents pursued the same line of attack, but the appeal of that critique with so many transplants and retirees populating the stretch from Charleston to Hilton Head Island is questionable. The local population has grown so rapidly in recent years that concerns about overdevelopment have become a potent political issue. Lacore has criticized Honeycutt for her work representing developers in the area. “There are more people in my town now who are not from here than there are people who are natives,” Will Haynie, the mayor of Mount Pleasant, a Charleston suburb, told me. Many newcomers to the area are, like Lacore, military service members. “That is not a disqualifier,” he said. Haynie, a Republican, endorsed Lacore early in her campaign. He had backed Mace when she first ran for the seat, in 2020, but he’s become disenchanted with the Trump administration and told me he was looking for a Democrat who would fight for the area’s needs and help restore the balance of power between Congress and the presidency. “I was looking for a Democrat that I could trust, a Democrat who’s a proven leader, and a Democrat who I think would be very independent,” Haynie said. “I didn’t just do this as a political stunt.” During her veterans’ event, Lacore leveled nearly as much criticism at Mace as at Honeycutt, saying the district had long been “ignored” by Mace. Voters there spoke of their representative with open disgust and noted approvingly that Lacore struck them as everything Mace was not. “The longer she was involved in politics, the crazier she got,” Gary Gould, a 73-year-old retired consultant, told me of Mace. Lacore, by contrast, “dripped character and credibility,” he said. “It seems like she knows her way around Washington without being tainted by being a politician.” Honeycutt’s campaign did not make her available for an interview. Mace, however, responded to an inquiry almost immediately. She defended her popularity in the area, noting that she had brought hundreds of millions of dollars to the district and won her most recent race, in 2024, easily—her margin of 16 points outperformed Trump. (That election, however, came before she launched a high-profile crusade against the first openly transgender person elected to the House, Representative Sarah McBride; before she allegedly berated airport security officers; and before the publication of stories in which colleagues and associates described her as “unstable” and “unhinged.”) Mace took issue with both Lacore’s and Honeycutt’s messaging about her. “If somebody wants to call me clickbait politics,” Mace told me, or say that she’s “ignoring the district, I’d hate to see what they think their definition of serving it is, and I would hate to see how they would navigate attacks by the establishment on their record.” [ Read: The GOP’s culture-war Hail Mary ] Mace has raised concerns about the GOP’s standing in South Carolina’s Senate race, in which nervous Republican groups have begun spending on behalf of Senator Darline Graham—sister of the late Lindsey Graham. But Mace is supporting Honeycutt and believes she’ll defeat Lacore. “I think she’ll win handily,” Mace said. “She has been in the community a very long time.” Lacore’s other liability could be some lingering resentment from a contentious primary. She won with the help of significant outside spending from Democratic groups such as the Bench, which has backed some of the party’s most prominent recruits, including James Talarico in Texas, Josh Turek in Iowa, and Adam Hamilton in Kansas. Lacore’s top rival in the primary, Mac Deford, has yet to endorse her candidacy, and when I spoke with him at a gathering of Democrats in Charleston, he told me he had not yet seen her campaign aggressively enough among people “who traditionally do not vote for Democrats.” (A Lacore spokesperson responded: “I would invite Mac to come to the many events we’re doing in every corner of the district where a bipartisan coalition of voters is showing their support.”) Lacore has significantly outraised Honeycutt, and the Democrats’ main House super PAC has reserved ad money for a late push on her behalf. Republicans remain confident that they’ll retain the seat, though their allies are spending as if it might be at risk. A spokesperson for the GOP’s House campaign committee told me Democrats are wasting money on a “solidly Republican” seat. (The Cook Political Report lists it as “likely Republican.”) Democrats last week circulated a poll showing Lacore narrowly ahead of Honeycutt, but they aren’t quite predicting victory, either. “Anybody who tells you it’s not a tough district doesn’t know what they’re talking about,” John Moffett, a Charleston-based Democratic strategist, told me. But, he said, “if there’s a candidate that can win this race right now, it’s Nancy Lacore.” Judging from the polling nationwide, the ingredients are in place for a blue wave. In South Carolina, both parties are wondering if it will be big enough to carry Lacore to Congress.

items.title: Bignona : un boutiquier interpellé pour des faits présumés de viols répétés sur des mineurs
items.description: Le Commissariat urbain de Bignona a interpellé, le 15 octobre 2026, un individu soupçonné d’actes contre nature, de viols répétés sur des mineurs et de pédophilie. Cinq victimes présumées, toutes mineures, ont été identifiées à ce stade de l’enquête, selon la Police nationale. L’affaire fait suite à l’exploitation, le 12 octobre 2026, d’un renseignement opérationnel signalant des faits présumés d’agression sexuelle sur un mineur de 17 ans, qui auraient été commis par un boutiquier établi à Tenghori. Les investigations menées par les éléments du commissariat ont ensuite fait état de soupçons selon lesquels le mis en cause aurait attiré de jeunes garçons dans son commerce en leur offrant des biens matériels et des denrées alimentaires, dans le but présumé d’obtenir des relations sexuelles. Un déplacement sur les lieux a été effectué dans le cadre des investigations. Entendue en présence de son tuteur, la première victime présumée a déclaré que le suspect lui aurait offert un téléphone portable de marque iPhone XR avant de la contraindre à entretenir des relations sexuelles avec lui. Selon son témoignage, les faits se seraient produits à trois reprises dans la chambre du mis en cause. Le mineur a également indiqué avoir laissé sa tablette électronique allumée dans l’antichambre du suspect. L’appareil a été retrouvé lors de l’intervention policière. Après notification de son droit à un avocat, le suspect a été interpellé et conduit dans les locaux du commissariat pour les besoins de l’enquête. À ce stade de la procédure, cinq victimes présumées, toutes mineures, ont été identifiées, selon les informations communiquées par la Police nationale.

items.title: Bénin: 249,5 milliards de F CFA pour les routes, l’agriculture et l’électricité
items.description: Le Bénin a signé, les 12 et 13 octobre 2026 à Bangkok, trois accords de financement d’un montant global de 249,5 milliards de F CFA avec la Banque islamique de développement (BID) et la Banque arabe pour le développement économique en Afrique (BADEA). Ces ressources sont destinées à soutenir des projets structurants dans les infrastructures routières, l’agriculture et l’électrification, trois secteurs clés du développement économique et social du pays. Le Bénin renforce ses capacités de financement de projets prioritaires. En marge des Assemblées annuelles de la Banque mondiale et du Fonds monétaire international (FMI), organisées à Bangkok, les autorités béninoises ont conclu trois accords avec la BID et la BADEA, pour une enveloppe totale de 249,5 milliards de F CFA, soit plus de 380 millions d’euros. La plus grande part de ces financements, soit 201,3 milliards de F CFA apportés par la BID, est consacrée aux infrastructures routières. Elle servira à aménager et à élargir à quatre voies l’axe Godomey–Ouidah–Hillacondji, sur environ 94 kilomètres. Ce tronçon constitue un maillon stratégique du corridor Abidjan–Lagos, essentiel à la circulation des personnes et au développement des échanges commerciaux en Afrique de l’Ouest. Le projet s’inscrit dans un programme global évalué à 373,2 milliards de F CFA, qui prévoit également 60 milliards de F CFA de la Banque ouest-africaine de développement (BOAD) pour le tronçon Ouidah–Guézin, ainsi qu’un financement de 111,9 milliards de F CFA en cours auprès de la Banque africaine de développement (BAD) pour la section Comè–Grand-Popo. L’agriculture et l’électrification au cœur des investissements En complément des infrastructures routières, 12,5 milliards de F CFA sont destinés à l’intensification durable des systèmes agricoles fondés sur les légumineuses. Le projet vise à améliorer la fertilité des sols, à accroître la productivité des exploitations et à augmenter les revenus des petits producteurs. Sa mise en œuvre concernera 48 communes réparties dans cinq pôles de développement agricole. L’initiative entend ainsi contribuer à la consolidation des activités agricoles grâce à des systèmes de production plus performants et durables. Le secteur de l’électricité bénéficiera, quant à lui, d’une enveloppe de 35,75 milliards de F CFA pour étendre le réseau à 127 localités. Cette opération devrait permettre de raccorder plus de 61 000 ménages, ainsi que des services publics et de petites entreprises, contribuant à améliorer l’accès à l’énergie et à soutenir les activités économiques locales. Des financements pour accélérer le développement À travers ces trois accords, le Bénin mise sur des investissements ciblés pour renforcer ses infrastructures, soutenir la production agricole et élargir l’accès à l’électricité. Au-delà des montants mobilisés, l’enjeu réside dans la mise en œuvre effective des projets et les retombées concrètes attendues pour les populations. La réalisation de ces investissements sera déterminante pour traduire les engagements financiers en infrastructures fonctionnelles, en meilleures conditions de production agricole et en un accès élargi à l’énergie, au bénéfice du développement économique et social du Bénin. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Bénin: 249,5 milliards de F CFA pour les routes, l’agriculture et l’électricité est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Guinée : le PNUD réaffirme son engagement à accompagner la mise en œuvre du PND 2024-2040
items.description: Le Programme des Nations unies pour le développement (PNUD) entend poursuivre son accompagnement de la Guinée dans la mise en œuvre de son Programme national de développement (PND) 2024-2040, à travers l’appui aux politiques publiques, les projets pilotes et l’innovation. C’est ce qu’a indiqué son représentant résident en Guinée, Anthony Ohemeng-Boamah, ce vendredi 16 octobre 2026, au siège de l’institution à Coléah, à Conakry. S’exprimant à l’occasion d’un déjeuner de presse consacré à la présentation du rapport annuel 2025 du PNUD Guinée, Anthony Ohemeng-Boamah a précisé que l’action de l’institution s’inscrit dans les priorités de développement définies par les autorités guinéennes, plutôt que dans un programme indépendant de celui du pays. À cet effet, il a rappelé que le PNUD avait accompagné l’élaboration du PND 2024-2040, avec pour objectif de veiller à la prise en compte des engagements internationaux de la Guinée, notamment en matière de gouvernance, d’équité, d’inclusion, de genre et de jeunesse. « Nous ne pouvons pas tout faire », a-t-il souligné, expliquant que l’institution définit son propre cadre de coopération en tenant compte des orientations nationales. Celui-ci repose sur trois grands domaines : l’environnement, la gouvernance ainsi que la transformation socio-économique et numérique. Des politiques publiques aux actions de terrain Pour le représentant résident, l’accompagnement du PNUD se traduit d’abord par un appui à la conception des politiques et des stratégies publiques. En collaboration avec les ministères concernés, l’institution aide les autorités à définir des orientations claires pour conduire les transformations nécessaires au développement du pays. Le deuxième volet concerne les interventions de terrain visant à améliorer les conditions de vie des populations. Il peut s’agir, entre autres, de projets destinés à consolider la paix dans les zones affectées par des conflits, d’initiatives en faveur des femmes exerçant des activités agricoles ou encore d’actions pour aider les communautés à mieux gérer les effets du changement climatique et à préserver leurs écosystèmes. À ces interventions s’ajoute le recours à l’innovation et aux technologies pour renforcer la gestion des ressources naturelles et soutenir la transformation économique. Concilier exploitation minière et protection de l’environnement Anthony Ohemeng-Boamah a notamment insisté sur le rôle des outils technologiques dans le suivi des activités minières et la surveillance de leurs conséquences environnementales. Selon lui, ces innovations peuvent permettre aux autorités de mieux suivre les opérations sur les sites miniers, tout en veillant à ce que l’exploitation des ressources contribue effectivement au développement économique, sans compromettre l’environnement. « Tous ces bénéfices, l’être humain, les mines, l’agriculture, tout dépend de l’environnement », a-t-il fait remarquer, soulignant également la nécessité de concilier valorisation des ressources naturelles et préservation des écosystèmes. À travers cet accompagnement, le PNUD mise donc sur une approche combinant l’appui institutionnel, les projets pilotes, les initiatives génératrices de revenus et l’innovation technologique. L’objectif affiché est de soutenir la Guinée dans la réalisation de ses ambitions de développement à long terme, en veillant à ce que les politiques publiques et les investissements se traduisent par des améliorations concrètes dans la vie des citoyens.

items.title: KP Governor Kundi announces amended welfare scheme for police officers, martyrs’ families
items.description: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi on Friday announced changes to the compensation packages for police officers martyred or injured in the line of duty as part of efforts to promote peace in the province. The provincial government has increased compensation for the families of martyred police officers and amended the previous plot allotment scheme, opting to pay the families cash in lieu of plots. Under the new scheme, the families of martyred constables, head constables, assistant sub-inspectors (ASIs), sub-inspectors (SIs) and inspectors will receive Rs17 million in compensation, up from Rs11 million. For the families of martyred deputy superintendents of police (DSPs) and assistant superintendents of police (ASPs), compensation will increase from Rs16 million to Rs25 million. The families of martyred superintendents of police (SP), senior superintendents of police (SSP), assistant inspector general (AIG) and all grade 18 and 19 officers previously received Rs21m in compensation, but under the new scheme, they will receive Rs30m. For families of martyred deputy inspector generals (DIG), inspector generals of police (IGP) and grade 20 officers, the compensation would increase from Rs21m to Rs35m. Regarding compensation for injured police officers, Kundi said an increase should have been made earlier, but it had not been. To address this, he said, the government had made “significant increases” in compensation for officers who had been severely injured or permanently disabled in the line of duty. Previously, compensation for permanent disability stood at Rs500,000. His government had increased it tenfold to Rs5 million. Compensation for severe injuries had also been increased from Rs100,000 to Rs1.5m. Kundi added that the families of martyred police officers had previously been allotted plots. However, the scheme had proved inconvenient for some families, as those living in Dera Ismail Khan or Bannu might be allotted plots in Nowshera or Swabi. Under the new scheme, the families would receive financial compensation in lieu of plots. He stressed that cash payments would give the families the freedom to decide how to use the money, whether to rent a house or buy a plot or a house in a location of their choice. For the families of martyred constables and head constables, the government will provide Rs18 million in cash in lieu of a five-marla plot. The families of martyred ASIs, SIs and inspectors will receive Rs25m in cash instead of a seven-marla plot. Kundi further said that the families of DSPs and ASPs, who were previously entitled to a 10-marla plot, would now receive Rs30m in cash. For the families of officers of SP or SSP rank and above, compensation had been set at Rs70m in cash in lieu of a one-kanal plot. Kundi stressed that not only serving police officers but also their families were at risk. Noting that terrorists could target officers’ families, he said the government had decided to introduce a new compensation package for such incidents. If a police officer’s spouse or children were killed, the family would receive Rs5m in compensation. If an officer’s parents or siblings were killed, the government would pay Rs3m in compensation. Kundi also announced a compensation package for police officers who were killed while off duty. The families of constables, head constables, ASIs and inspectors killed while off duty would receive Rs4m. The compensation for the families of DSPs and ASPs killed while off duty had been set at Rs5m. For the families of SPs, SSPs and officers in grades 18 and 19, compensation had been set at Rs7m. The KP government has also announced Rs1m in compensation to help fund the weddings of martyred officers’ daughters, describing it as “essential financial assistance at an important stage of the families’ lives”, Kundi said. Children of martyred officers will also benefit from a new fund being established to support their education, including studies abroad, Kundi said. The governor added that salaries of KP police officers had been increased by more than expected in an effort to make their pay packages more attractive than those offered in other provinces. He added that he had directed the relevant officials to expedite recruitment to the KP police, which has 17,000 vacancies. Concluding his remarks, Kundi said: “The days of rifts between the Centre and the province are gone. We now have to work together for the province’s peace and prosperity.” Kundi had on Tuesday directed the authorities to prepare and submit, at the earliest, a summary containing proposals for an increase in police salaries and an enhanced welfare package for the families of police martyrs. Chairing a high-level meeting at the Governor House, he reviewed proposals relating to police salaries and welfare measures for the families of martyred and injured police personnel. On Oct 11, the federal government imposed emergency and governor’s rule in KP, under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, making Kundi the leader of the province.
